Synset.Definition: Planned or emergency care provided to a child or adult with a special need in order to provide temporary relief to the family caregiver of that child or adult

Services designed to assist individuals in acquiring, retaining, and improving the self-help, socialization, and adaptive skills necessary to reside successfully in home and community based settings; includes (with exceptions) prevocational, educational, and supported employment services, but does not include special education and related services available to the individual through a local educational agency or vocational rehabilitation services available through a program funded under section 730 of title 29

Services which will assist individuals eligible under the State Medicaid plan in gaining access to needed medical, social, educational, and other services, including assessment of an eligible individual to determine service needs, development of a specific care plan, referral and related activities to help an individual obtain needed services, and monitoring and followup activities to ensure the care plan is effectively implemented and adequately addresses the needs of the individual; case management is covered under this distinct statutory authority, not as a personal care service or a home health care service, so it is not one of the two service categories reached by the electronic visit verification requirement

The waiver authority under which the Secretary may provide that a State Medicaid plan include as medical assistance payment for part or all of the cost of home or community-based services (other than room and board), approved by the Secretary, which are provided pursuant to a written plan of care to individuals with respect to whom there has been a determination that but for the provision of such services the individuals would require the level of care provided in a hospital or a nursing facility or intermediate care facility for the mentally retarded (the statute's own facility term; current regulations say intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities) the cost of which could be reimbursed under the State plan

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396n(b), (c); 42 USC 1315; Medicaid.gov, "Home & Community Based Services Authorities" (distinguishing waiver authorities from state plan options)
Synset.Definition: A general term for several distinct federal authorities under which the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) permits a state to waive certain otherwise-mandatory federal Medicaid requirements (such as statewideness, comparability of services, or freedom of choice of provider) so the state can operate a more targeted or flexible program. The two waiver authorities most relevant to home-and-community-based caregiving are 1915(b) waivers (Social Security Act § 1915(b), 42 USC 1396n(b)), which let a state waive freedom-of-choice requirements to deliver services through a managed-care delivery system, and 1915(c) Home and Community-Based Services waivers (§ 1915(c), 42 USC 1396n(c)), which let a state cover home and community-based services, otherwise unavailable under the ordinary Medicaid state plan, for individuals who would otherwise require an institutional level of care. A state may also combine a 1915(b) and a 1915(c) waiver ("1915(b)/(c) combination waiver") to deliver HCBS through managed care. Separately, and under different statutory authority, section 1115 demonstration waivers (Social Security Act § 1115, 42 USC 1315) let CMS approve broader, experimental state pilot programs that would otherwise violate Medicaid's federal requirements, evaluated for research and demonstration purposes rather than tied to a specific service category. Related Medicaid HCBS options that expand a state's own state plan rather than waiving federal requirements -- for example, the 1915(i) HCBS state plan option and the 1915(k) Community First Choice option -- are not, strictly, "waivers" in this sense, since they do not require CMS to waive a statutory requirement

With respect to personal care services or home health care services, a system under which visits conducted as part of such services are electronically verified with respect to the type of service performed, the individual receiving the service, the date of the service, the location of service delivery, the individual providing the service, and the time the service begins and ends

The requirement (section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act) that, with respect to any amount expended for personal care services or home health care services requiring an in-home visit by a provider under a State Medicaid plan or waiver, unless the State requires the use of an electronic visit verification system for such services, the Federal medical assistance percentage is reduced on an escalating schedule: for personal care services furnished in calendar quarters beginning on or after January 1, 2020 (.25 percentage points in 2020, rising to 1 percentage point for 2023 and each year thereafter), and for home health care services furnished on or after January 1, 2023
For purposes of the electronic visit verification requirement, services described in section 1396d(a)(7) of title 42 provided under a State Medicaid plan (or under a waiver of the plan)

Services, not otherwise furnished under the State's Medicaid plan, that are furnished under a waiver granted under 42 CFR part 441, subpart G. They may include case management services, homemaker services, home health aide services, personal care services, adult day health services, habilitation services, respite care services, day treatment or other partial hospitalization services, psychosocial rehabilitation services and clinic services for individuals with chronic mental illness, and other services requested by the State agency and approved by CMS as cost effective and necessary to avoid institutionalization

Synset.dc:source: CMS 1915(c) Waiver Technical Guide v3.6 (Jan. 2019), Appendix C (Homemaker) (elaborated definition)
Synset.Definition: Services that consist of the performance of general household tasks (for example, meal preparation and routine household care) provided by a qualified homemaker, when the individual regularly responsible for these activities is temporarily absent or unable to manage the home and care for him or herself or others in the home; listed as one of the services a State may cover under a Medicaid HCBS waiver at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(2)

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 409.45(b); listed as a waiver service at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(3)
Synset.Definition: Visits by a home health aide to provide hands-on personal care, or services needed to maintain the person's health or facilitate treatment of an illness or injury — for example bathing, dressing, grooming, hair, nail and oral hygiene, feeding, assistance with elimination, assistance with ambulation, changing position in bed, and assistance with transfers

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 440.167; listed as a waiver service at 42 CFR 440.180(b)(4)
Synset.Definition: Services furnished to an individual who is not an inpatient or resident of a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities, or institution for mental disease, that are authorized for the individual by a physician in accordance with a plan of treatment or, at the option of the State, otherwise authorized in accordance with a service plan approved by the State; provided by an individual who is qualified to provide the services and who is not a member of the individual's family; and furnished in a home, and at the State's option, in another location; for EVV purposes, 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(C) covers personal care services provided under a State plan, including services provided under section 1396d(a)(24), 1396n(c), 1396n(i), 1396n(j), or 1396n(k) of this title, or under a section 1315 waiver

The initial evaluation of an individual's need for the level of care provided in a hospital, a nursing facility, or an intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (required when there is a reasonable indication that the individual might need such services in the near future), together with periodic reevaluations, at least annually, of each beneficiary receiving home or community-based services to confirm the continued need for that level of care

The process for developing an individual's person-centered service plan, which must be led by the individual (and the individual's authorized representative, if applicable); include people chosen by the individual; provide necessary information and support to ensure the individual directs the process to the maximum extent possible; occur at times and locations convenient to the individual; reflect cultural considerations and use plain language; include strategies for solving conflict or disagreement; offer informed choices regarding services and supports; and exclude providers of HCBS for the individual from developing the plan, except under the limited conflict-of-interest exception where no other willing and qualified entity is available

The written plan produced by the person-centered planning process, which must reflect the services and supports that address the individual's identified functional needs and preferences, including the setting in which the individual resides as chosen by the individual; the individual's strengths and preferences; clinical and support needs identified through an assessment of functional need; individually identified goals and desired outcomes; the services and supports (paid and unpaid) and the providers of them, including natural supports; and risk factors and measures in place to minimize them; written in plain language and finalized with the individual's informed written consent

The requirement that providers of HCBS for an individual, or those who have an interest in or are employed by a provider of HCBS for the individual, must not provide case management or develop the person-centered service plan, except when the State demonstrates that the only willing and qualified entity to provide case management or develop plans in a geographic area also provides HCBS, with conflict-of-interest protections approved by CMS

Case management services furnished without regard to the statewide-provision requirements of 42 CFR 431.50(b) and the comparability requirements of 42 CFR 440.240, allowing a State to offer the services to individuals in any defined location of the State or to individuals within targeted groups specified in the State plan

Habilitation services that prepare an individual for paid or unpaid employment and that are not job-task oriented but are aimed at a generalized result — such as teaching concepts of compliance, attendance, task completion, problem solving, and safety — rather than at teaching skills for a specific job

Habilitation services — including special supervisory services, training, transportation, and adaptive equipment — that facilitate paid employment for individuals for whom competitive employment is unlikely and who, because of their disabilities, need intensive ongoing support to perform in a work setting

The CMS final rule published May 10, 2024 (89 FR 40542; effective July 9, 2024) that amended Medicaid regulations to improve access to care across fee-for-service, managed care, and home and community-based services, including the HCBS payment adequacy (80 percent direct care worker compensation) requirement, incident management system and critical incident requirements, grievance systems for fee-for-service HCBS, the HCBS Quality Measure Set, and payment rate transparency requirements

For purposes of the HCBS payment adequacy requirement, a direct care worker's salary, wages, and other remuneration as defined by the Fair Labor Standards Act and implementing regulations; benefits (such as health and dental benefits, life and disability insurance, paid leave, retirement, and tuition reimbursement); and the employer share of payroll taxes for direct care workers delivering services authorized under section 1915(c)

Costs that are not included in the calculation of the percentage of Medicaid payments to providers that is spent on compensation for direct care workers under the HCBS payment adequacy requirement; limited to costs of required trainings for direct care workers, travel costs for direct care workers (such as mileage reimbursement or public transportation subsidies), and costs of personal protective equipment for direct care workers

The requirement that a State ensure each provider spends at least 80 percent of total Medicaid payments it receives for homemaker services, home health aide services, and personal care services on total compensation for the direct care workers who furnish those services; excluded costs (required trainings, travel, and personal protective equipment) are not counted in the calculation. Adopted in the 2024 Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services final rule

An incident that a State must, at a minimum, define to include: verbal, physical, sexual, psychological, or emotional abuse; neglect; exploitation including financial exploitation; misuse or unauthorized use of restrictive interventions or seclusion; a medication error resulting in a telephone call to, or a consultation with, a poison control center, an emergency department visit, an urgent care visit, a hospitalization, or death; or an unexplained or unanticipated death, including but not limited to a death caused by abuse or neglect
A system that the State must operate and maintain for its Medicaid HCBS programs that identifies, reports, triages, investigates, resolves, tracks, and trends critical incidents

Procedures a State must establish under which beneficiaries receiving HCBS through a fee-for-service delivery system may file a grievance related to the State's or a provider's performance of the person-centered planning and HCBS settings requirements; the State must resolve each grievance within 90 calendar days of receipt, extendable by up to 14 calendar days, with decisions made by individuals not involved in prior review who have appropriate expertise

An expression of dissatisfaction about any matter other than an adverse benefit determination; grievances may include, but are not limited to, the quality of care or services provided and aspects of interpersonal relationships

In Medicaid managed care, a determination by a plan that includes: the denial or limited authorization of a requested service; the reduction, suspension, or termination of a previously authorized service; or the denial, in whole or in part, of payment for a service, among other determinations enumerated in the regulation

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 441.312(b)(2) (defining the measure set); 42 CFR 441.312(a), (c)-(g) (use-and-reporting mandate)
Synset.Definition: The Home and Community-Based Services Quality Measures for Medicaid established and updated by the Secretary through a process that allows for public input and comment; States operating section 1915(c) waiver programs must use it and report mandatory measures to CMS in a standardized form and manner, with certain measures stratified by demographic factors on a phased timeline
The requirement that a State publish all Medicaid fee-for-service fee schedule payment rates on a website accessible to the general public, with updates required within one month of a rate change

An advisory group that a State must establish — including, at a minimum, direct care workers, beneficiaries, beneficiaries' authorized representatives, and other interested parties — to advise and consult on Medicaid fee-for-service payment rates for homemaker, home health aide, personal care, and habilitation services and the sufficiency of those rates; the group must meet at least every two years

A setting that qualifies for Medicaid HCBS because it is integrated in and supports full access of individuals receiving HCBS to the greater community, including opportunities to seek employment and work in competitive integrated settings; is selected by the individual from among setting options including non-disability-specific settings; ensures rights of privacy, dignity, respect, and freedom from coercion and restraint; optimizes individual initiative, autonomy, and independence; and facilitates individual choice regarding services and supports and who provides them. Provider-owned or controlled residential settings must additionally provide a legally enforceable residency agreement with eviction protections, privacy in the unit including lockable doors, choice of roommates, control over schedules and visitors, and physical accessibility

The process by which the Secretary determines, based on information presented by the State or other parties, whether a setting presumed to have institutional qualities — such as a setting in a building also used for inpatient institutional treatment, a setting on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution, or a setting that has the effect of isolating individuals from the broader community — may nonetheless qualify as a home and community-based setting

Under the Medicaid Access Rule, any of the following individuals who deliver home and community-based services (employed or contracted by a Medicaid provider, State agency, or third party, or working under a self-directed model): a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist providing nursing services; a licensed or certified nursing assistant; a direct support professional; a personal care attendant; a home health aide; or other individuals paid to provide services addressing activities of daily living or instrumental activities of daily living, behavioral supports, employment supports, or other services to promote community integration

Synset.dc:source: President's Committee for People with Intellectual Disabilities, Report to the President 2017 (elaborated definition)
Synset.Definition: A direct care worker who provides services and supports that empower people with intellectual and developmental disabilities to live, work, and participate in the community, such as assistance with daily living, employment supports, and community integration; listed as a direct-care-worker category at 42 CFR 441.302(k)(1)(ii)(C)

The adequate standards for all types of providers that furnish services under an HCBS waiver, which the State must assure are met as a safeguard for beneficiary health and welfare, including that the standards of any applicable State licensure or certification requirements are met for services or for individuals furnishing services

A screening that a State Medicaid agency must require as a condition of provider enrollment: providers must consent to criminal background checks, including fingerprinting when required under State law or by the level of screening based on risk of fraud, waste, or abuse determined for the provider category; a provider, or a person with a 5 percent or more direct or indirect ownership interest in the provider, determined to be high risk must submit a set of fingerprints within 30 days upon request from CMS or the State Medicaid agency

Under Virginia law, a "barrier crime" is a conviction, disqualifying a person from employment or volunteer service with a qualified entity that provides care to children, the aged, or the disabled, falling into one of six categories: (i) specified violent, sexual, and abuse- or neglect-related felony and misdemeanor offenses under Title 18.2 of the Code of Virginia, or a substantially similar offense under the law of another jurisdiction; (ii) burglary and related breaking-and-entering offenses (Va. Code §§ 18.2-89 through 18.2-94), or a substantially similar offense elsewhere; (iii) specified felony controlled-substance and alcohol offenses, or a substantially similar offense elsewhere; (iv) a felony violation of § 18.2-250 (drug possession), or a substantially similar offense elsewhere; (v) an offense requiring registration on Virginia's Sex Offender and Crimes Against Minors Registry; or (vi) any other felony not included in clauses (i) through (v), unless five years have elapsed since the conviction

The individual-employee-level criminal background screening a long-term-care facility or provider (including a home health agency, hospice, or personal-care-services provider) performs on a prospective "direct patient access employee" -- any individual who has, or may have, one-on-one contact with a patient or resident through employment or contract with the facility or provider -- before that individual works directly with patients or residents. This is distinct from the separate, provider/business-enrollment-level screening under 42 CFR 455.434 (which reaches the provider entity and its high-risk owners, not individual direct-care employees). The federal touchstone for this individual-level screening is the National Background Check Program, established by § 6201 of the Affordable Care Act (Pub. L. 111-148) and codified at 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7l: a voluntary CMS grant program, not a universal federal mandate, that funded a subset of states (roughly half) to develop a standardized state screening procedure combining a fingerprint-based check through the FBI's Integrated Automated Fingerprint Identification System with a search of state-based abuse and neglect registries and databases, including the abuse and neglect registry of any other state where the prospective employee previously resided. Outside a state that adopted an NBCP-style program, the specific criminal-history-screening procedure, disqualifying-offense list, and fingerprinting requirement for individual direct-care workers are set by that state's own law rather than by a single uniform federal rule

Vermont's confidential state registry, maintained by the Department of Disabilities, Aging and Independent Living's Division of Licensing and Protection (Adult Protective Services), listing the name, the date of the finding, and the nature of the finding for every caregiver found, on the basis of a substantiated Adult Protective Services report, to have abused, neglected, or exploited a vulnerable adult. An employer of a caregiver for children or vulnerable adults may query the registry to check a specific prospective or current employee before hiring or continuing to employ that individual; the registry exists specifically to let such employers screen individuals who would otherwise directly access a vulnerable population. Being listed reflects a substantiated finding, not a mere allegation. This registry is functionally the same kind of state-based abuse and neglect registry the National Background Check Program's own screening procedure requires a participating state to search when vetting a prospective direct patient access employee who previously resided in that state
The Federal Government's share of a State's expenditures under the Medicaid program
A bill for services, a line item of service, or all services for one beneficiary within a bill

A claim that can be processed without obtaining additional information from the provider of the service or from a third party; States must pay 90 percent of all clean claims from practitioners (in individual or group practice or practicing in shared health facilities) within 30 days of receipt and 99 percent within 90 days of receipt

The information relating to the receipt of any item(s) or service(s) by an enrollee under a contract between a State and a managed care organization (MCO), prepaid inpatient health plan (PIHP), or prepaid ambulatory health plan (PAHP) that is subject to the requirements of 42 CFR 438.242 and 438.818; States must validate encounter data for accuracy and completeness before submitting it to CMS
Approval from a health plan that may be required before you get a service or fill a prescription in order for the service or prescription to be covered by your plan
An intentional deception or misrepresentation made by a person with the knowledge that the deception could result in some unauthorized benefit to himself or some other person

Provider practices that are inconsistent with sound fiscal, business, or medical practices, and that result in unnecessary cost to the Medicaid program or in reimbursement for services that are not medically necessary or that fail to meet professionally recognized standards for health care; it also includes beneficiary practices that result in unnecessary cost to the Medicaid program. Distinct from abuse of a person, which is a category of critical incident under 42 CFR 441.302(a)(6), and from elder abuse as defined at 42 USC 3002(1)

The Secretary shall exclude from participation in any Federal health care program any individual or entity that has been convicted of: a criminal offense related to the delivery of an item or service under Medicare (subchapter XVIII) or under any State health care program; a criminal offense, under Federal or State law, relating to neglect or abuse of patients in connection with the delivery of a health care item or service; for an offense occurring after August 21, 1996, a felony, under Federal or State law, relating to fraud, theft, embezzlement, breach of fiduciary responsibility, or other financial misconduct in connection with the delivery of a health care item or service or with respect to any act or omission in a government-operated or government-financed health care program; or, for an offense occurring after August 21, 1996, a felony, under Federal or State law, relating to the unlawful manufacture, distribution, prescription, or dispensing of a controlled substance

The Secretary may exclude from participation in any Federal health care program individuals and entities including: for an offense occurring after August 21, 1996, those convicted, under Federal or State law, of a misdemeanor relating to fraud, theft, embezzlement, breach of fiduciary responsibility, or other financial misconduct, either in connection with the delivery of a health care item or service or with respect to any act or omission in a government-operated or government-financed program; those convicted of obstructing an investigation or audit; those convicted of a misdemeanor relating to a controlled substance; those whose license to provide health care has been revoked, suspended, or surrendered; and other individuals and entities enumerated by statute for excessive claims, kickbacks, and related program-integrity violations

An allegation of fraud that has been verified by the State, which may come from any source — including fraud hotline tips verified by further evidence, claims data mining, and patterns identified through provider audits, civil false claims cases, and law enforcement investigations. Allegations are considered credible when they have indicia of reliability and the State Medicaid agency has reviewed all allegations, facts, and evidence carefully and acts judiciously on a case-by-case basis

Synset.dc:source: 31 USC 3729(a)(1), (b)(1) (Title 31 is not a loaded USC title)
Synset.Definition: The federal statute (31 USC 3729-3733) imposing civil liability on any person who knowingly presents, or causes to be presented, a false or fraudulent claim for payment or approval, or who knowingly makes, uses, or causes to be made or used, a false record or statement material to a false or fraudulent claim; knowingly means having actual knowledge of the information, acting in deliberate ignorance of its truth or falsity, or acting in reckless disregard of its truth or falsity; violations carry treble damages plus civil penalties

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(1), (5)(B), (5)(C); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (bundled/alternate-titled-service and managed-care/fee-for-service-parity guidance)
Synset.Definition: A Medicaid service within the scope of the electronic visit verification requirement: a personal care service or a home health care service requiring an in-home visit by a provider under a State plan or waiver, for which a State must require the use of an electronic visit verification system or forfeit a portion of the Federal medical assistance percentage; only these two service categories are reached by 42 USC 1396b(l), and the requirement applies equally whether the service is furnished through a fee-for-service or a managed care delivery system, and even where the service is bundled into, or billed under, a differently-named service, so long as the underlying service meets the personal-care-service or home-health-care-service definition; there is no separate federal list of covered services by name — the test is definitional, not a named list

Any of the six data points that an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services — the type of service performed, the individual receiving the service, the date of the service, the location of service delivery, the individual providing the service, and the time the service begins and ends; the statutory enumeration is exhaustive

Synset.dc:source: 21st Century Cures Act sec. 12006(c)(2), Pub. L. 114-255
Synset.Definition: A technology used to electronically capture and verify the six required data elements of an electronic visit verification visit; the 21st Century Cures Act bars requiring the use of any particular or uniform system, so a State may adopt any method that verifies those elements, subject to CMS's own auditability requirements — commonly a mobile application, telephony, or a fixed in-home device

The type of service performed — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

The individual receiving the service — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

The date of the service — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

The location of service delivery — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

The individual providing the service — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

The time the service begins and ends — one of the six elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify for a visit conducted as part of personal care services or home health care services

Synset.dc:source: New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs (self-attributing this capture-method category to CMS guidance); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (CMS's own use of "tablets"/"phones" as EVV implementation tools, in its enhanced-federal-match guidance)
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification capture method using a smartphone- or tablet-based application, downloaded by the caregiver, that records the service period and captures location at visit check-in and check-out

Synset.dc:source: New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs (self-attributing this capture-method category to CMS guidance)
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification capture method in which the caregiver places a telephone call to record the start and end of a visit and verify the location of service delivery, using a landline telephone, a fixed Voice-over-Internet-Protocol phone tied to the recipient's address, or (paired with a fixed in-home device for location) a cell phone

Synset.dc:source: New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs (self-attributing this capture-method category to CMS guidance); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (CMS's own use of "fobs" as an EVV implementation tool, in its enhanced-federal-match guidance)
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification capture method using a stationary hardware device installed in the service recipient's home that generates a unique time-stamped code to verify the caregiver's presence at check-in and check-out, used independently or paired with a phone-based method that cannot itself confirm a fixed address; "fixed object device" (FOB), "fixed visit verification device" (FVV) and "alternative device" are vendor and state terms for this device category

Synset.dc:source: IBM, "What Is Interactive Voice Response (IVR)?" (technology glossary)
Synset.Definition: An automated telephony system that interacts with callers using pre-recorded voice prompts and telephone-keypad or voice input, gathering information or routing a call without a live agent; a generic telecommunications term, not specific to EVV or Medicaid law, used in electronic visit verification as a common implementation of telephony-based capture

An electronic visit verification system used by a provider that is not operated by the State or by a contractor on behalf of the State; a State may require personal care service and home health care service providers to utilize such a system, in which case the enhanced federal financial participation available for a State-operated system (90 percent for design, development, or installation and 75 percent for operation and maintenance) does not apply

The delivery of a health care service to an individual by telecommunication rather than by a provider physically present with the individual; because 42 USC 1396b(l)(1) triggers the electronic visit verification requirement only for personal care services or home health care services requiring an in-home visit by a provider, a service delivered by telehealth does not satisfy that in-home-visit predicate and is not within EVV scope

Hospice care means the care described in section 1395x(dd)(1) of this title, furnished by a hospice program to a terminally ill individual who has voluntarily elected to have payment made for hospice care instead of having payment made for certain other benefits; it is a distinct optional Medicaid benefit category, not one of the two service categories reached by the electronic visit verification requirement (home health care services under 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(B) or personal care services under 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(C))

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(B)-(C); North Carolina Medicaid EVV FAQ (state corroboration that EVV is not required for ABA therapy)
Synset.Definition: A behavioral-health treatment for autism spectrum and related disorders, typically covered as a distinct Medicaid behavioral-health or EPSDT benefit; it is not among the services described in 42 USC 1396d(a)(7) (home health care services, cross-referenced by 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(B)) nor within the personal care services category of 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(C), so it is not within the electronic visit verification scope

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(1); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (institutional-resident exclusion; separately, the congregate/24-hour/per-diem-billed-setting exclusion)
Synset.Definition: A congregate or institutional residential setting — such as a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities, an institution for mental diseases, an assisted living facility, an assisted living program, or other residential care facility — that is not an individual's own private home; 42 USC 1396b(l)(1) triggers the electronic visit verification requirement only for personal care services or home health care services requiring an in-home visit by a provider. Personal care services furnished to an inpatient or resident of a hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities, or an institution for mental diseases are not subject to the requirement; separately, CMS guidance interprets "in-home visit" to exclude personal care services furnished in a congregate residential setting where 24-hour service is available, because such settings are typically reimbursed on a per diem rather than a discrete per-visit basis

Synset.dc:source: CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Additional EVV Guidance" (Aug. 8, 2019), FAQ Q1 (interpreting 42 USC 1396b(l))
Synset.Definition: A scope carve-out recognized by CMS guidance: personal care services or home health care services rendered by an individual who lives in the same residence as the beneficiary do not constitute an in-home visit, so such services are not federally required to be verified through an electronic visit verification system, although a State may nonetheless choose to require EVV for live-in caregivers

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(A); CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Additional EVV Guidance" (Aug. 8, 2019), FAQ Q3; New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs (applying this rule to Community Habilitation specifically)
Synset.Definition: When a single visit for a personal care service or home health care service occurs partly in an individual's home and partly in the community, the electronic visit verification requirement reaches only the portion of the visit rendered in the home; a State may capture the specific location where the service starts and stops regardless of whether it is in the home or the community, may instead record the location data element as either "home" or "community" without transmitting the specific community location, or may capture only the home location together with the start and stop time of the full service unit — worker shifts that begin in the home and end in the community, or the reverse, likewise require EVV only for the home portion of the shift. This is the general rule that resolves a service delivered partly in the community, including a Community Habilitation service claim: the claim does not require EVV reporting if the services being claimed are delivered entirely in the community, but does require it to the extent any portion is delivered in the home

Synset.dc:source: CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Additional EVV Guidance" (Aug. 8, 2019), FAQ Q2 (superseding an earlier, more general May 2018 CMS FAQ answer on the same topic)
Synset.Definition: The component of the Medicaid home health benefit authorizing the provision of a medical supply, equipment, or appliance is outside electronic visit verification scope: the delivery, set-up, and/or instruction on the use of a medical supply, equipment, or appliance does not constitute an "in-home visit," regardless of whether that delivery, set-up, or instruction occurs in the beneficiary's home

Medical social services and dietary or nutrition counseling furnished by a social worker or dietitian making a home visit; neither is included in the Medicaid home health services regulation's exhaustive list of covered services — nursing service, home health aide service, medical supplies and equipment, and, at the State's option, physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services — so neither falls within the home health care services category cross-referenced by the electronic visit verification requirement

Synset.dc:source: Alabama Medicaid, "Alabama Medicaid's Electronic Visit Verification and Monitoring System (EVVM), Frequently Asked Questions" (June 23, 2017)
Synset.Definition: Alabama Medicaid's own name — Electronic Visit Verification and Monitoring (EVVM) — for its State implementation of the federal electronic visit verification requirement: an electronic scheduling, tracking, reporting, and billing system for in-home care providers, historically operated for Alabama as AuthentiCare® Alabama; a State-specific program name, not a distinct federal or CMS term

Synset.dc:source: CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (confirming no beneficiary-side connectivity requirement)
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification system does not require a Medicaid beneficiary to have an Internet connection, a cell phone, or a landline; a State may select an EVV system option that meets the six required data elements without relying on the beneficiary to supply any technology, including an option in which the provider — not the beneficiary — has a phone or electronic tracker available to staff

Synset.dc:source: North Carolina Medicaid, Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Frequently Asked Questions (May 22, 2024); North Carolina Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy No. 3A (Home Health Services), Section 7.6.2 ("Coordination with In-Home Drug Infusion Therapy")
Synset.Definition: Home infusion therapy -- the administration of drugs or biologicals intravenously or subcutaneously in the home, coordinated with, but billed as a distinct service from, home health nursing -- is not subject to electronic visit verification, per North Carolina Medicaid's own administrative coordination policy for this service; this is a state Medicaid agency's own coverage-policy determination, not a uniform federal CMS rule of general application

Under IDEA, "early intervention services" means developmental services that are provided under public supervision; are provided at no cost except where Federal or State law provides for a system of payments by families, including a schedule of sliding fees; are designed to meet the developmental needs of an infant or toddler with a disability, in any one or more of physical development, cognitive development, communication development, social or emotional development, and adaptive development; and are provided in conformity with an individualized family service plan

A written statement for a child with a disability, developed, reviewed, and revised by an IEP Team (which includes the child's parents, at least one regular and one special education teacher, a local educational agency representative, and, where appropriate, the child), that must include: the child's present levels of academic achievement and functional performance, including how the disability affects involvement and progress in the general education curriculum; measurable annual academic and functional goals; a description of how progress toward those goals will be measured and reported; the special education, related services, and supplementary aids and services to be provided; the extent, if any, to which the child will not participate with nondisabled children in the regular class and other school activities; any individual accommodations needed for State or districtwide assessments, or, if the child will take an alternate assessment, why and which one; and the projected start date, frequency, location, and duration of services. Beginning with the first IEP in effect when the child turns 16, and updated annually thereafter, the IEP must also include appropriate measurable postsecondary goals and the transition services needed to reach them

Nursing services for beneficiaries who require more individual and continuous care than is available from a visiting nurse or routinely provided by the nursing staff of a hospital or skilled nursing facility; private duty nursing is a distinct optional Medicaid state-plan service under 42 USC 1396d(a)(8) and 42 CFR 440.80, separate from the home health care services category (42 USC 1396d(a)(7)) that 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(B) cross-references, so it does not by itself fall within the home-health electronic visit verification definition

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(A); 21st Century Cures Act sec. 12006(c)(2), Pub. L. 114-255; CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (GPS/Interactive-Voice-Response and location-privacy guidance); CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Electronic Visit Verification" (May 16, 2018), "EVV Models" section
Synset.Definition: The global positioning system; there is no requirement to use GPS to satisfy the electronic visit verification location requirement — GPS is one optional approach for capturing the location of service delivery, not itself a required data element, the statutory element being the location of service delivery, and a common alternative is Interactive Voice Response. Federal law does not mandate GPS, but the technology-neutrality requirement bars CMS from mandating that a State use a particular or uniform system, rather than barring a State or provider from selecting one, so a State's or provider's own chosen electronic visit verification system may itself require GPS as its location-capture method

A worker's or beneficiary's Social Security number; it is not among the six data elements an electronic visit verification system must electronically verify (type of service, individual receiving the service, date, location of service delivery, individual providing the service, and time the service begins and ends), the statutory enumeration being exhaustive

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(5)(A); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018) (location-privacy guidance)
Synset.Definition: The continuous capture of an individual's location as the individual moves through the community; the Cures Act does not require a State to capture each location as an individual moves through the community — capturing the location where a home-based service starts and stops is sufficient to meet the location-of-service-delivery element

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(1); CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Additional EVV Guidance" (Aug. 8, 2019), FAQ #4
Synset.Definition: A paper or manual timesheet; it does not satisfy the electronic visit verification requirement, which requires an electronic system — CMS guidance confirms that even web-based timesheets alone, without independent auditable confirmation of the data entered by the provider and approved by the individual, are not sufficient to electronically verify the six required data elements, so a paper timesheet, which is not electronic at all, likewise cannot satisfy the requirement

Synset.dc:source: U.S. Dept. of Health and Human Services, Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC), healthit.gov, "EMR vs EHR"
Synset.Definition: A digital version of the paper charts in a clinician's office, containing the medical and treatment history of the patients in one practice; a clinical documentation system distinct in purpose and content from an electronic visit verification system, which verifies operational facts about the occurrence of a visit

A qualified electronic health record: an electronic record of health-related information on an individual that includes patient demographic and clinical health information, such as medical history and problem lists; has the capacity to provide clinical decision support, support physician order entry, capture and query information relevant to health care quality, and exchange and integrate electronic health information from other sources; and includes, or is capable of including, a real-time benefit tool that conveys patient-specific real-time cost and coverage information with respect to prescription drugs; a clinical health-IT system distinct from an electronic visit verification system

Synset.dc:source: New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs; Pennsylvania Dept. of Human Services EVV FAQ (attributing the aggregation function to CMS guidance)
Synset.Definition: A State-designated centralized system that collects, validates, and stores electronic visit verification data submitted by the different EVV systems used within a State — a State-operated system and any alternate or third-party systems providers use — standardizing the data before it is used for Medicaid claims processing and federal reporting

A limited first-year exception under which the Federal medical assistance percentage reduction for lacking an electronic visit verification system does not apply — for personal care services, for calendar quarters in 2020, and for home health care services, for calendar quarters in 2023 — for a State that demonstrates to the Secretary that it has made a good faith effort to comply (including by taking steps to adopt the technology used for an electronic visit verification system) and, in implementing such a system, has encountered unavoidable system delays

An entity a State may use to provide financial management services to participants self-directing personal assistance services, performing functions such as collecting and processing worker timesheets; processing payroll and the withholding, filing, and payment of applicable employment-related taxes and insurance; maintaining a separate account for each participant's budget; tracking and reporting disbursements and balances of participant funds; processing and paying invoices for approved goods and services; and providing participants periodic reports of expenditures and the status of the approved budget; commonly called a Financial Management Services Agency (FMSA) in state Medicaid self-direction programs

Synset.dc:source: CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Electronic Visit Verification" (May 16, 2018), "Integrate EVV Systems with Other State Medicaid Systems and Data" section; New York State Dept. of Health EVV FAQs (confirming EVV submissions and claims are submitted separately and are not used to auto-generate a claim)
Synset.Definition: In an electronic visit verification system, the record of a Medicaid beneficiary's approved service type and units or hours, drawn from the beneficiary's service or care plan, against which electronically verified visit data is matched for claims payment; a claim generated in excess of the authorized service amount is reduced in payment to the amount authorized and confirmed by the visit data. Distinct from prior authorization (a health plan's approval that a service will be covered before it is rendered). Electronic visit verification data and claims data are matched, not merged: an electronic visit verification system does not itself generate or replace a Medicaid claim, and visit data and claims are submitted through separate processes

Synset.dc:source: CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Electronic Visit Verification" (May 16, 2018), "Define EVV Requirements" section, p. 9
Synset.Definition: An occurrence in which data required to be recorded and reported for an electronic visit verification visit is missing or invalid — for example, a check-in for a scheduled visit with no matching check-out, a caregiver entering an incorrect EVV identifier, or a caregiver checking in from an unconfirmed phone number and therefore unable to establish presence — which a provider must manually clear before the visit can be confirmed

Synset.dc:source: CMCS Informational Bulletin, "Electronic Visit Verification" (May 16, 2018), "Define EVV Requirements" section, p. 9
Synset.Definition: The manual clearing by a provider of missing or invalid electronic visit verification check-in or check-out data, required to confirm a visit whose electronically captured record is incomplete or cannot establish that the required data elements were met

An individual who has been determined eligible and is currently receiving Medicaid; the current Medicaid regulatory term for the person receiving services (the pre-ACA term "recipient", still used colloquially in many state EVV programs, is not itself a currently defined regulatory term)

The hospital insurance benefits program under Part A of title XVIII of the Social Security Act, providing insurance against the costs of inpatient hospital services, post-hospital extended care services, home health services, and hospice care

Medicare Part A coverage of skilled nursing and rehabilitation care furnished to a hospital inpatient after transfer to a participating skilled nursing facility, conditioned on a prior qualifying hospital stay, a level-of-care requirement, and a per-benefit-period day limit; also called post-hospital extended care services

The items and services covered under the SNF benefit when furnished to a hospital-transferred SNF inpatient: nursing care by or under the supervision of a registered nurse; bed and board furnished in connection with that nursing care; physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology services; medical social services; drugs, biologicals, supplies, appliances, and equipment; and other services necessary to the health of patients that skilled nursing facilities generally provide

The optional Medicare Part A benefit under which a beneficiary who is entitled to Part A and has been certified as terminally ill may elect to receive hospice care -- the comprehensive, interdisciplinary palliative items and services (nursing care, physical/occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, medical social services, home health aide and homemaker services, medical supplies including drugs and biologicals, physicians' services, short-term inpatient care including respite care, counseling including dietary and bereavement counseling, and any other item or service specified in the plan of care) furnished to a terminally ill individual by, or by others under arrangements made by, a Medicare-certified hospice program under a written plan of care established and periodically reviewed by the individual's attending physician, the hospice medical director, and the hospice's interdisciplinary group -- elected by the beneficiary instead of standard Medicare coverage of certain other benefits related to the terminal illness

A public agency or private organization (or subdivision of either) that is primarily engaged in furnishing hospice care as defined in 42 USC 1395x(dd)(1), available on a 24-hour basis, that provides bereavement counseling for the immediate family of the terminally ill individuals it serves, and that furnishes hospice care directly or under arrangements in the individual's home, on an outpatient basis, and on a short-term inpatient basis, meeting CMS's hospice conditions of participation

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 418.3 (defining "Terminally ill"); 42 USC 1395x(dd)(3)(A); 42 CFR 418.21 (benefit-period structure); 42 CFR 418.22(a)(1) (recertification required for each period)
Synset.Definition: The clinical/legal status of an individual with a medical prognosis that his or her life expectancy is 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course -- a prospective prognosis standard assessed at the time of certification, not a retrospective judgment of how long the individual actually survives; outliving an earlier 6-month prognosis does not by itself disqualify a beneficiary from continued hospice care, since each hospice benefit period requires only a fresh recertification of the same prospective standard

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1395x(dd)(3)(B); 42 USC 1395f(a)(7)(A)(i) (two-physician certification structure); 42 CFR 418.3 (defining "physician designee")
Synset.Definition: The physician (as defined at 42 USC 1395x(r)(1)), nurse practitioner (42 USC 1395x(aa)(5)), or physician assistant -- who may be employed by the hospice -- whom the individual identifies as having had the most significant role in determining and delivering the individual's medical care at the time the individual elects hospice care; distinct from the hospice medical director or physician designee, who acts on the hospice's own interdisciplinary-group side of certification

A beneficiary is eligible to elect the Medicare hospice benefit only if the beneficiary is (a) entitled to Medicare Part A, and (b) certified as terminally ill in accordance with the certification procedure

The written (or, in narrow timing exceptions, initially oral) attestation required for every hospice benefit period, including recertification for each subsequent period even under an unlimited-duration election, that the individual's prognosis is a life expectancy of 6 months or less if the terminal illness runs its normal course, based on the certifying physician's clinical judgment and accompanied by a brief clinical narrative. For the initial 90-day period, certification requires both the hospice medical director (or physician designee, or an interdisciplinary-group physician member) and the individual's attending physician, if the individual has one; for each subsequent period, certification by the hospice-side physician alone suffices

Beginning with the third hospice benefit period and before every subsequent recertification thereafter, a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must conduct a face-to-face encounter with the individual to gather clinical findings supporting continued eligibility, and must attest in writing that the encounter occurred; CMS uses this requirement as its program-integrity check on long-stay hospice patients rather than as any hard cutoff on the length of hospice care

The mechanism by which an eligible beneficiary (or representative, if the individual is mentally or physically incapacitated) elects the Medicare hospice benefit by filing a signed election statement with a chosen hospice, identifying that hospice and the individual's attending physician, acknowledging the palliative rather than curative nature of hospice care as it relates to the individual's terminal illness and related conditions, and acknowledging which Medicare services are thereby waived

For the duration of a hospice election, the beneficiary waives Medicare payment for (1) hospice care from any hospice other than the one elected, absent arrangement by that hospice, and (2) any Medicare services related to the treatment of the terminal condition for which hospice was elected, or a related condition, or that are equivalent to hospice care -- except services furnished by the designated hospice itself, by another hospice under arrangement, or by the individual's own attending physician if that physician is not a hospice employee or receiving hospice compensation. Where the hospice determines that specific conditions, items, services, or drugs are unrelated to the individual's terminal illness and related conditions, the individual (or representative), a non-hospice provider furnishing them, or a Medicare contractor may request a written addendum -- titled "Patient Notification of Hospice Non-Covered Items, Services, and Drugs" -- listing them as remaining separately billable outside the hospice benefit

A beneficiary may elect hospice care across, in strict sequence, an initial 90-day period, a subsequent 90-day period, and an unlimited number of subsequent 60-day periods, available only in that order; each period requires its own physician certification or recertification of a continued 6-month-or-less prognosis. Distinct from the general Medicare Part A benefit period (spell of illness) governing inpatient hospital and SNF coverage, which resets after 60 consecutive days outside a hospital or SNF -- a hospice benefit period is instead one of a sequence of elected periods within a single ongoing hospice election and has no comparable 60-day reset

A hospice election is treated as continuing without a break across the initial and subsequent benefit periods -- a single ongoing election, not a fresh election each period -- as long as the individual remains under the hospice's care, does not revoke the election, and is not discharged. (42 CFR 418.22(a)(1) cross-references this continuation rule to "§ 418.24(c)", but current § 418.24(c) is the hospice election-statement-addendum provision, not the continuation provision -- the continuation rule actually appears at § 418.24(f), a stale internal cross-reference left uncorrected across two separate CMS rulemakings that each inserted new subsections into § 418.24: a 2019 rule that added the addendum-content provision, and a 2021 rule that added both an addendum-timeframes provision and an unrelated notice-of-election filing-deadline provision, without ever updating this pointer.)

The individual (or representative) may revoke the hospice election at any time during a benefit period by filing a signed statement with the hospice, specifying an effective date no earlier than the date of the revocation itself. Upon revocation the individual is no longer covered under Medicare for hospice care, resumes standard Medicare coverage of the benefits that had been waived, and may elect hospice again at any time thereafter for any other benefit period still available. The hospice must file notice of the revocation with its Medicare contractor within 5 calendar days of the effective date, unless a final claim was already filed. (42 CFR 418.28(c)(2) cross-references the resumed-coverage rule to "§ 418.24(f)(2)", but current § 418.24(f)(2) is the "does not revoke the election" clause of the continuity provision, not a benefits-waiver provision -- the waiver-of-other-benefits provision it evidently means to point to is now § 418.24(g)(2), the same stale-pointer pattern as § 418.22(a)(1).)

Following a revocation, the individual (or representative, if the individual is mentally or physically incapacitated) may at any time file a new hospice election, under the same election procedure, for any other election period still available to the individual

Hospice eligibility is not automatically terminated by a beneficiary surviving beyond the six months of the original prognosis. Because hospice benefit periods recur without a fixed cap -- an unlimited number of subsequent 60-day periods -- and each period requires only a fresh physician recertification of a continuing 6-month-or-less prognosis, not a backward-looking check on whether an earlier prognosis "came true," hospice care may continue indefinitely as long as recertification keeps supporting the prognosis at each interval. The face-to-face-encounter requirement, which activates specifically at the third benefit period and every recertification thereafter, functions as CMS's program-integrity check on exactly this long-stay scenario rather than a hard six-month cutoff -- a conclusion drawn from these provisions together, not stated in any single section in so many words

A group or groups of individuals designated by a Medicare-certified hospice that furnish and, collectively, supervise the hospice's care and services, addressing the physical, medical, psychosocial, emotional, and spiritual needs of hospice patients and their families; the hospice separately designates one of the group's registered nurses to coordinate care and ensure continuous assessment of each patient's and family's needs. A hospice's interdisciplinary group must include, at minimum: a physician who is an employee of, or under contract with, the hospice; a registered nurse; a social worker, marriage and family therapist, or mental health counselor; and a pastoral or other counselor qualified to address spiritual needs

A hospice team member who provides hands-on personal-care services to the patient under the plan of care and the general supervision of a registered nurse, and who -- together with hospice homemaker services providing household-maintenance assistance and services enabling the individual to carry out the treatment plan -- is a covered hospice service distinct from core interdisciplinary-group membership. A hospice aide must complete at least 75 combined hours of classroom and supervised practical training (at least 16 hours of classroom instruction before at least 16 hours of supervised practical training), pass a competency evaluation performed by a registered nurse in consultation with other skilled professionals as appropriate, and receive at least 12 hours of in-service training every 12-month period; a registered nurse must also make an on-site visit to the patient's home no less frequently than every 14 days to assess the quality of care and services the aide is providing (the aide need not be present for this visit), and a separate on-site visit at least annually to directly observe the aide while actually performing care

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 418.64(d)(1); defined term "Bereavement counseling" at 42 CFR 418.3
Synset.Definition: A hospice condition-of-participation core service: an organized bereavement-support program, supervised by a qualified professional, providing emotional, psychosocial, and spiritual support and services to the patient's family and other individuals identified in the bereavement plan of care, both before and after the patient's death, to assist with grief, loss, and adjustment; services must be available for up to one year following the patient's death and, where appropriate, extended to residents of the facility where the patient resided

Medicare-certified hospices are required to use volunteers, under the supervision of a designated hospice employee, to provide day-to-day administrative and/or direct patient-care services in an amount that, at minimum, equals 5 percent of the total patient-care hours of all paid hospice employees and contract staff; hospices must also provide volunteer orientation and training, document ongoing recruiting and retention efforts, and demonstrate cost savings attributable to volunteer use

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 418.202(a)-(i); core-services condition of participation at 42 CFR 418.64
Synset.Definition: The items and services covered under the Medicare hospice benefit: (a) nursing care by or under the supervision of a registered nurse; (b) medical social services under a physician's direction; (c) physicians' services, including those of the hospice medical director or physician interdisciplinary-group member; (d) counseling services, including dietary counseling, for the individual and family/caregivers; (e) short-term inpatient care, including respite care, in a participating hospice inpatient unit, hospital, or skilled nursing facility; (f) medical appliances and supplies, including drugs and biologicals used primarily for relief of pain and symptom control related to the terminal illness; (g) home health aide and homemaker services; (h) physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech-language pathology services; and (i) any other service specified in the plan of care as reasonable and necessary for palliation or management of the terminal illness and related conditions. A narrower subset of this list -- nursing, medical social, and counseling services -- must additionally be routinely furnished directly by the hospice's own employees, rather than under arrangement, as a separate hospice condition of participation; physician services, by contrast, may be furnished under contract

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 418.202(f); Center for Medicare Advocacy, "Hospice" (corroborating that hospice manages a patient's illness and pain rather than treating the underlying terminal illness)
Synset.Definition: Electing hospice does not mean a beneficiary stops receiving all medical care or medication. What changes is the goal of care for the terminal illness and related conditions: hospice replaces standard Medicare coverage of curative, disease-directed treatment for the terminal illness with palliative care focused on comfort and symptom management, delivered by the hospice's interdisciplinary team; only drugs used primarily for the relief of pain and symptom control related to the individual's terminal illness are covered as part of the hospice benefit, but Medicare coverage for health problems unrelated to the terminal illness continues outside the hospice per-diem, and comfort-focused treatment of the terminal illness itself is exactly what hospice is designed to provide, not what a patient gives up

Synset.dc:source: Sykes N, Thorns A., "The use of opioids and sedatives at the end of life," Lancet Oncology 2003;4(5):312-318; Portenoy RK et al., "Opioid use and survival at the end of life: a survey of a hospice population," J Pain Symptom Manage 2006;32(6):532-540; von Gunten CF, "Morphine and Hastened Death," Fast Facts and Concepts #8, 3rd ed., Palliative Care Network of Wisconsin (rev. May 2015); American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine, Position Statement on Palliative Sedation (2014) (scoped to continuous palliative sedation, not routine opioid analgesia)
Synset.Definition: Whether hospice, or the opioid and sedative medications commonly used in hospice for pain and symptom control, hastens death is a widespread lay concern that the peer-reviewed clinical literature does not support when dosing is properly titrated for symptom control: a clinical review of the evidence and the largest United States hospice cohort study of the question found no association between opioid or sedative use, dose, or dose escalation and earlier death in hospice populations. The "doctrine of double effect" -- the ethical principle that a treatment intended to relieve suffering can be permissible even if it foreseeably risks an unintended harmful side effect -- is frequently invoked to justify opioid use near the end of life, but part of the clinical-ethics literature argues the doctrine is over-applied to properly-dosed morphine specifically, because the empirical risk of hastening death from titrated dosing is minimal rather than a genuine trade-off; hospice/palliative medicine's own professional body retains the same intent-based ethical reasoning for more aggressive interventions such as continuous palliative sedation, requiring clinicians to be clear in their intent to palliate symptoms and not to shorten survival, though its own position statement does not invoke the doctrine of double effect by name. This is an actively-discussed question in clinical ethics rather than a settled matter in either direction, and the correction here concerns appropriately-titrated, symptom-focused dosing specifically, not a claim that opioid pharmacology carries no risk at excessive or rapidly-escalated doses

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 418.3 (defining "Palliative care", a hospice-context regulatory definition, not a general-purpose federal definition of palliative care outside Part 418); 42 CFR 418.22(b)(1) (certification); 42 CFR 418.24(b)(2) (election to forgo curative treatment); 42 CFR 418.24(g)(2) (operationalizing that election as a waiver of other Medicare benefits); Center to Advance Palliative Care, "Palliative Care Definition"; National Coalition for Hospice and Palliative Care, Clinical Practice Guidelines for Quality Palliative Care, 4th ed. (2018)
Synset.Definition: Patient- and family-centered care that optimizes quality of life by anticipating, preventing, and treating suffering, addressing physical, intellectual, emotional, social, and spiritual needs throughout the continuum of illness; unlike hospice, palliative care is based on the patient's needs rather than the patient's prognosis, is appropriate at any age and at any stage of a serious illness, and can be provided together with curative treatment. Hospice is a specific, regulated type of palliative care: it additionally requires a certified terminal prognosis of six months or less and an election to forgo standard Medicare coverage of curative treatment for the terminal condition, so every hospice patient receives palliative care but most palliative-care patients are not hospice patients

Synset.dc:source: Reisberg B., "Functional assessment staging (FAST)," Psychopharmacology Bulletin 1988;24(4):653-659
Synset.Definition: A clinician-administered ordinal staging instrument assessing the sequential loss of functional, activities-of-daily-living capacity characteristic of Alzheimer's disease and other primary degenerative dementias, describing a continuum of successive stages and lettered substages from Stage 1 (no functional decline, normal adult) through Stage 6 (marked by progressive loss of the ability to dress, bathe, and use the toilet independently, and by urinary and fecal incontinence) and Stage 7 (the most severe stage, subdivided into substages 7a-7f, marked by progressive loss of speech, ambulation, and postural control); a patient's assigned FAST stage tracks the ordinal severity of dementia-related functional impairment independent of, though correlated with, cognitive test scores

Synset.dc:source: CMS Local Coverage Determination L34538, "Hospice Determining Terminal Status" (CGS Administrators, LLC), Section II.B, revision effective 09/26/2019
Synset.Definition: The Medicare hospice local coverage determination test for whether a beneficiary with a primary diagnosis of dementia due to Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder has a life expectancy of six months or less. Under CMS Local Coverage Determination L34538 ("Hospice Determining Terminal Status," CGS Administrators LLC, Jurisdiction J-15), a beneficiary must show ALL of: FAST stage seven or beyond; inability to ambulate without assistance; inability to dress without assistance; inability to bathe without assistance; urinary and fecal incontinence (intermittent or constant); and no consistently meaningful verbal communication, limited to stereotyped phrases or six or fewer intelligible words -- AND must additionally have had at least ONE of the following within the preceding 12 months: aspiration pneumonia; pyelonephritis or other upper urinary tract infection; septicemia; multiple stage 3-4 decubitus ulcers; recurrent fever after antibiotics; or an inability to maintain sufficient fluid and calorie intake, evidenced by 10 percent weight loss over the preceding six months or serum albumin below 2.5 gm/dl. FAST stage seven alone, without a qualifying comorbid complication, does NOT satisfy this guideline; the guideline is stated as a "should"-standard given great weight on review, not an absolute bar, so a physician may still certify terminal status on other documented clinical grounds even where this specific checklist is not fully met. The LCD's own text does not use the substage label "7c" -- it says "Stage seven or beyond" and separately itemizes the functional/verbal criteria above; "FAST 7c" is common secondary/hospice-industry shorthand for this criteria cluster, not LCD-defined terminology. L34538 is Jurisdiction J-15's own Medicare Administrative Contractor LCD; other MACs maintain parallel LCDs with substantively similar dementia criteria under different LCD numbers, not independently verified word-for-word here

Synset.dc:source: 26 U.S.C. § 21(a), (c), (d)(1)-(2); 26 CFR 1.21-1(a)(1); IRS Publication 503 (2025); the 2026-forward percentage formula was amended by Pub. L. 119-21 ("One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), § 70405
Synset.Definition: A nonrefundable federal income tax credit equal to an "applicable percentage" of employment-related expenses paid for the care of a qualifying person so the taxpayer (and spouse, if filing jointly) can work or look for work: for tax years through 2025, 35 percent of expenses, reduced by 1 point for each $2,000 of adjusted gross income above $15,000, down to a 20 percent floor first reached above $43,000 AGI; for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, 50 percent, reduced by 1 point per $2,000 of AGI above $15,000 to a 35 percent floor first reached above $43,000 AGI (a flat plateau from roughly $43,001 to $75,000 AGI), then, for AGI above $75,000 ($150,000 on a joint return), further reduced by 1 point per $2,000 ($4,000 joint) to a 20 percent floor not reached until AGI exceeds $103,000 ($206,000 joint) -- the 20 percent rate does not begin the instant AGI crosses $75,000/$150,000, only the second phase-down does. Expenses taken into account are capped at $3,000 for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more, and cannot exceed the taxpayer's own earned income (or, if married, the lower-earning spouse's earned income, subject to a deemed-income rule for a spouse who is a full-time student or incapable of self-care). Claimed on Form 2441, attached to Form 1040, with the credit entered on Schedule 3

An individual whose care expenses may be taken into account for the Child and Dependent Care Credit: (A) the taxpayer's dependent under age 13; (B) the taxpayer's dependent, or a person who would be the taxpayer's dependent except that the person's gross income was too high (for 2025, $5,200 or more, a figure indexed annually), filed a joint return, or could be claimed as a dependent by someone else, who is physically or mentally incapable of self-care and shares the taxpayer's principal place of abode for more than half the year; or (C) the taxpayer's spouse, if physically or mentally incapable of self-care and sharing the taxpayer's principal place of abode for more than half the year. A person is "physically or mentally incapable of self-care" if, because of a physical or mental defect, the person cannot attend to their own hygiene or nutritional needs, or requires full-time attention for their own safety or others' safety; an inability to work, keep house, or care for children does not by itself establish incapacity for self-care

An amount paid for household services or for the care of a qualifying person that is "employment-related" only if it enables the taxpayer (or spouse, if filing jointly) to work or actively look for work -- volunteer work or work for nominal pay does not count -- and it is for a qualifying person's care. Qualifying expenses include dependent care center fees (if the center complies with applicable state or local law), day camp (even a specialized day camp), before- and after-school care for a child in kindergarten or above, nursery school or preschool, care-provider-furnished transportation, and required agency or application fees. Expenses for overnight camp, for food, lodging, clothing, or education standing alone, for summer school or tutoring, or for care during an extended (not short and temporary) absence from work do not qualify, nor do amounts reimbursed under an employer plan or paid to the taxpayer's spouse or to the parent of the taxpayer's own qualifying child

Synset.dc:source: 20 CFR 416.1201(a)(1); 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4) (first-party and pooled trusts only)
Synset.Definition: A trust structure holding assets for the benefit of a person with a disability in a way that is not counted as an available resource for means-tested benefits such as Medicaid and SSI, because the beneficiary lacks the legal right or authority to liquidate the trust principal for their own support and maintenance; also called a "supplemental needs trust." Federal Medicaid law recognizes several distinct categories of special needs trust -- first-party, third-party, and pooled -- each with its own funding source, eligibility rule, and, where applicable, Medicaid payback obligation; 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4) governs only the first-party and pooled categories, not the third-party category, which instead falls under ordinary SSI/Medicaid trust principles

A "(d)(4)(A) trust": a trust containing the assets of an individual under age 65 who is disabled (as defined at 42 U.S.C. § 1382c(a)(3)) and established for the individual's benefit by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian, or a court, under which the state must receive all amounts remaining in the trust at the individual's death, up to the total medical assistance paid on the individual's behalf. Also called a self-settled or self-funded special needs trust, because it is funded with the beneficiary's own assets -- for example, an inheritance received outright or a personal-injury settlement.
