Before December 13, 2016, only a parent, grandparent, legal guardian, or a court could establish this trust; the Special Needs Trust Fairness Act (§ 5007 of the 21st Century Cures Act, Pub. L. 114-255) added "the individual" to that list, letting a disabled person with legal capacity establish their own. The trust must be established, and generally funded, before the beneficiary turns 65

A trust funded with assets that never belonged to the beneficiary -- for example, assets of a parent, grandparent, or other relative -- as opposed to a first-party trust, which is funded with the beneficiary's own assets. Because 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4) reaches only trusts "containing the assets of an individual" (the beneficiary), a third-party trust is not governed by that subsection and carries no federal Medicaid payback requirement; it is instead evaluated under ordinary SSI/Medicaid trust principles, under which trust principal is a countable resource only if the beneficiary has legal authority to revoke or terminate the trust and use the funds for their own food or shelter. At the beneficiary's death, remaining assets pass to named remainder beneficiaries rather than to the state. There is no dedicated federal statutory definition of the "third-party special needs trust" the way there is for the first-party and pooled trusts; it is a discretionary/spendthrift trust instrument drafted to satisfy these general SSI/Medicaid resource rules

A "(d)(4)(C) trust": a trust containing the assets of a disabled individual (as defined at 42 U.S.C. § 1382c(a)(3)) that is established and managed by a nonprofit association, maintains a separate account for each beneficiary while pooling the accounts for investment and management, is established for the sole benefit of disabled individuals by a parent, grandparent, legal guardian, the individual, or a court, and, to the extent amounts remaining in the beneficiary's account at death are not retained by the trust, pays the state from those remaining amounts up to the total medical assistance paid on the beneficiary's behalf. Unlike the first-party trust, a pooled trust has always allowed the beneficiary to establish their own account, and its statutory text contains no under-age-65 requirement for establishing an account. That does not mean funding is age-neutral, though: the separate transfer-of-assets penalty exemption for trusts, 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(c)(2)(B)(iv), by its own terms covers only a trust "for the sole benefit of an individual under 65 years of age who is disabled," so a transfer of the beneficiary's own assets into a pooled trust after age 65 falls outside that specific safe harbor; whether and how a state actually penalizes such a post-65 funding transfer varies, and has been separately litigated, so this is an unresolved area of state variation rather than a settled federal rule. Whether the trust manager retains some or all of a deceased beneficiary's remaining sub-account balance, rather than paying it to the state, is likewise a matter of the trust's own governing documents, subject to any more restrictive requirements a state imposes on pooled trusts operating in its Medicaid program

Synset.dc:source: 42 U.S.C. § 1395y(b)(2)(A)-(B); 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A)/(C); Center for Medicare Advocacy, and multiple MSP-compliance law-firm explainers (convergent secondary/practitioner characterization — CMS's own primary WCMSA Reference Guide text could not be independently fetched in this research pass, cms.gov having blocked automated retrieval)
Synset.Definition: A portion of a personal-injury or workers'-compensation settlement allocated to pay for future injury-related medical care that would otherwise be covered by Medicare, required to be exhausted and properly accounted for before Medicare resumes paying for related treatment; grounded in the Medicare Secondary Payer statute, under which Medicare may not pay for an item or service to the extent payment has been made or can reasonably be expected from a workers'-compensation plan, liability insurance, or group health plan, and any conditional Medicare payment made in the meantime must be reimbursed once the primary payer's responsibility is established. Because set-aside funds remain a countable, available asset to the settlement recipient, they can jeopardize Medicaid/SSI eligibility for a disabled recipient unless the set-aside is nested as a segregated sub-account inside a properly drafted first-party or pooled special needs trust -- an integration technique that combines the Medicare Secondary Payer statute with the Medicaid special-needs-trust provisions as a matter of standard settlement-planning practice, not itself a single named CMS or Medicaid rule. There is no statute or regulation requiring a WCMSA proposal to be submitted to CMS for review -- submission is a CMS-recommended, not legally mandated, process

A tax-advantaged savings account for an individual with a disability, created by the Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) Act of 2014 and codified at 26 U.S.C. § 529A: account earnings grow tax-free, and withdrawals used for the beneficiary's "qualified disability expenses," as defined at 26 U.S.C. § 529A(e)(5), are tax-free. An individual is eligible for a taxable year if entitled to Social Security disability or blindness benefits (Title II or XVI) with an onset before a statutory age threshold, or has an on-file disability certification; that threshold, currently age 46, was raised from age 26 effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, by the ABLE Age Adjustment Act, enacted as part of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-328). For SSI purposes, up to $100,000 of an ABLE account balance is excluded as a countable resource for the designated beneficiary; if the balance exceeds $100,000 and that excess causes the individual to exceed the overall SSI resource limit, SSI cash payments are suspended, not terminated, and Medicaid eligibility continues indefinitely during that suspension so long as the ABLE-driven excess is the sole cause of it. A distribution from an ABLE account, whether or not for a qualified disability expense, is treated as a conversion of a resource from one form to another, not as income

Under federal Medicaid trust rules, a trust an individual is deemed to have "established" -- funded, even partly, with the individual's own assets, whether created by the individual, the individual's spouse, an agent under a power of attorney, a guardian, or anyone acting at the individual's direction -- is treated very differently depending on whether it is revocable or irrevocable. A revocable trust receives no asset-protection treatment at all: its entire corpus is a countable resource of the individual, distributions to the individual are the individual's income, and any other distribution is treated as an uncompensated transfer of assets. An irrevocable trust is protected only to the extent that, under the "any circumstances" test, no payment could ever be made to or for the individual from that portion of the trust; if there is any scenario, however remote, under which the trustee could pay principal or income to the individual, that entire reachable portion remains a countable resource indefinitely. Establishing (funding) an irrevocable trust is not itself a way around Medicaid rules: the portion genuinely put beyond the individual's reach is treated, as of the date of funding, as an uncompensated transfer of assets subject to Medicaid's ordinary asset-transfer look-back period (see cg-look-back-period in the sibling caregiving_lexicon.xml), which today runs a uniform 60 months for essentially any transfer -- trust-funding or outright gift alike -- because the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 extended the 60-month look-back to "any other disposal of assets made on or after February 8, 2006," not only trust-related transfers; the 36-month figure survives in the statute's text only as a description of pre-2006 non-trust transfers, not as a current-law baseline that trust funding deviates from. The special needs trusts, qualified income trusts, and pooled trusts described elsewhere in this cluster are statutory exceptions carved out of this general rule, not additional applications of it

A trust, composed only of the individual's pension, Social Security, and other income (plus accumulated income in the trust), established in a state for the individual's benefit, under which the state must receive all amounts remaining in the trust at the individual's death, up to the total medical assistance paid on the individual's behalf; commonly called a "Miller trust." This device is available only in an "income cap" state -- one that does not otherwise operate a medically-needy nursing-facility spend-down pathway for institutional Medicaid; an applicant in such a state whose gross income exceeds the state's institutional-Medicaid income limit can become financially eligible by depositing income into this irrevocable trust each month, since the deposited income is then disregarded when the state tests income eligibility. The statute itself requires only income-only composition and the state payback on death; the specific categories of permitted monthly disbursement from the trust are set by CMS sub-regulatory guidance and state Medicaid agency policy, not spelled out in the statute

Synset.dc:source: 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(C); N.Y. State Dept. of Health/OPWDD program materials (GIS 19 MA/04); 18 NYCRR 360-4.5(b)(5); 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(10)(C) (the medically-needy nursing-facility pathway that excludes New York from qualified-income-trust eligibility under 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(B)(iii)); medicaidplanningassistance.org (convergence-tier only for the Connecticut and New-York/Connecticut-exclusivity characterization)
Synset.Definition: A pooled trust established and managed by a nonprofit association under 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(C), used specifically so a disabled Medicaid applicant with income above the community/HCBS eligibility limit can deposit that "surplus" or "excess" income into the trust each month instead of incurring a recurring medical-expense spend-down (see cg-spend-down/cg-medically-needy in the sibling caregiving_lexicon.xml); the deposited income is disregarded when the state budgets the individual's income for Medicaid eligibility, and remaining sub-account funds can be used for the beneficiary's ordinary living expenses, not only medical bills. New York's own program materials describe this mechanism, used there for exactly this purpose, as codified under 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(C) and implementing state regulation; at least one independent secondary source reports Connecticut operates the same mechanism for the same purpose, though this was not independently checked against a Connecticut primary source. "Medicaid Surplus" (also "Surplus Income Program") is informal, New York-specific branding, not a nationally standard legal term, and in practice covers two distinct, layered mechanisms that are easy to conflate: New York's own medically-needy excess-income spend-down pathway itself -- available because New York is not a hard-income-cap state, unlike the states that use a qualified income trust -- and, separately, this pooled trust, which lets a disabled applicant avoid that recurring spend-down obligation. Whether other states beyond New York and Connecticut operate a (d)(4)(C) pooled trust specifically for this ongoing income-budgeting purpose, rather than only for lump-sum asset protection, was not confirmed in this research

The amount of a Medicaid recipient's own income that must be applied each month to the cost of institutional or home-and-community-based-services care, computed by having the state reduce its payment to the facility or HCBS provider by whatever income remains after mandatory deductions: a personal needs allowance (a federal statutory floor of $30 a month for an individual, $60 a month for an institutionalized couple, though a state may set a higher amount, or, for HCBS, a broader "maintenance needs" allowance the state may set at any level supported by a reasonable-needs assessment, subject to a state-set maximum), a spousal maintenance needs allowance for a community spouse, a family maintenance needs allowance for other dependents remaining in the community, and incurred medical or remedial expenses not covered by a third party. Also called "patient participation." The applicable federal provision depends on setting and state type: institutional care in an SSI-criteria state (42 CFR 435.725), HCBS waiver care in an SSI-criteria state (42 CFR 435.726), institutional care in a state using more restrictive ("209(b)") income/resource rules than SSI (42 CFR 435.733), and HCBS waiver care in a 209(b) state (42 CFR 435.735)

Synset.dc:source: IRS Notice 2014-7, 2014-4 I.R.B. 445; 26 U.S.C. § 131(c)(2); IRS FAQ, "Certain Medicaid Waiver Payments May Be Excludable From Income" (Q1-Q6, Q9, Q12-Q14, Q19)
Synset.Definition: The federal income-tax exclusion, announced in IRS Notice 2014-7, under which certain payments received by an individual care provider under a state Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services waiver program (authorized under § 1915(c) of the Social Security Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1396n(c)) for nonmedical support services provided to an eligible individual, related or unrelated to the caregiver, living in the care provider's home are treated as excludable "difficulty of care payments" under 26 U.S.C. § 131, whether or not the caregiver is related to the care recipient. The exclusion turns on a "same home" test: it applies when the care recipient lives in the provider's home (including when the provider moved into the recipient's home to provide care, or when more than one caregiver lives with the recipient), but not when the provider maintains a separate residence and simply works at the recipient's home, and not to respite care given where the recipient does not live. It is also capped by the same numeric limits Section 131(c)(2) applies to qualified foster care generally: the exclusion covers payments for no more than 10 qualified individuals age 18 or under, or 5 qualified individuals age 19 or older, being cared for in the same home. Whether payments under a state program other than a § 1915(c) waiver (for example, many self-direction or Community First Choice programs) qualify depends on the specific nature, purpose, and design of that program -- it is not automatic. Excluding these payments from income tax is a separate legal question from whether they are subject to Social Security and Medicare (FICA) tax, which instead depends on whether the caregiver is an agency employee, an employee of the care recipient, or an independent contractor, subject to the ordinary domestic-service exceptions. A taxpayer may still choose, for an open tax year, to include all (not part) of these excluded payments as earned income for purposes of the Earned Income Tax Credit or the Additional Child Tax Credit, if the payments otherwise meet the statutory definition of earned income

The federal payroll tax imposed on wages under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA), 1.45 percent on the employee and 1.45 percent on the employer (2.9 percent combined), and its self-employment (SECA) equivalent, a 2.9 percent tax on net self-employment income; this base rate applies to a paid caregiver's wages or self-employment earnings regardless of whether some or all of those payments are separately excluded from income tax as difficulty-of-care payments, since the income-tax exclusion and the payroll-tax question are analyzed separately. Because the tax reaches only "wages" and "self-employment income," and those terms are statutorily defined to exclude distributions from qualified retirement plans (401(a), 403(a), 403(b) annuity plans, SEPs, and certain governmental plans), this base Medicare tax does not apply to a retiree's pension or 401(k)/IRA-type distributions; Social Security benefit payments likewise are not "wages" or self-employment income under any Code provision and so are outside the reach of this tax

An additional 0.9 percent Medicare tax imposed, on top of the base Medicare tax, on wages and self-employment income above $250,000 on a joint return, $125,000 for a married taxpayer filing separately, or $200,000 in any other case; unlike the base Medicare tax, it is not split between employee and employer -- it falls on the individual alone. It applies to the same wage and self-employment income base as the base Medicare tax, so it likewise does not reach Social Security benefits or qualified retirement-plan distributions, and a coordination rule prevents the same self-employment dollars from being counted toward both the wage-side and self-employment thresholds. These dollar thresholds are not indexed for inflation and have been unchanged since the tax's 2013 enactment

Synset.dc:source: 26 U.S.C. § 1411(a)-(c); IRS, "Questions and Answers on the Net Investment Income Tax," Q9, Q14; IRS, "Questions and Answers for the Additional Medicare Tax."
Synset.Definition: A distinct 3.8 percent tax, legally unrelated to FICA/SECA despite sometimes being colloquially grouped with "Medicare taxes," imposed under 26 U.S.C. § 1411 on the lesser of an individual's net investment income or the amount by which modified adjusted gross income exceeds $250,000 on a joint return, $125,000 for a married taxpayer filing separately, or $200,000 in any other case -- the same, also non-inflation-indexed, thresholds as the Additional Medicare Tax. Net investment income is interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, rents, and certain trade/business or property-disposition gain -- not wages, not self-employment income, and, by explicit statutory exclusion, not a distribution from a 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408, 408A, or 457(b) plan. IRS guidance confirms Social Security benefits and qualified-plan distributions are not net investment income, and that this tax and the Additional Medicare Tax never apply to the same dollar of income: the 0.9 percent Additional Medicare Tax reaches wages, compensation, and self-employment income, while this 3.8 percent tax reaches investment income such as interest, dividends, capital gains, and rental income -- so investment income earned during retirement can trigger this tax above the MAGI thresholds even though it never triggers Medicare or SECA tax at all

A federal law, 29 U.S.C. Chapter 28, that entitles an eligible employee of a covered employer to job-protected leave for specified family and medical reasons and requires the employer to maintain the employee's group health insurance coverage during the leave on the same terms as if the employee had not taken leave. The standard entitlement is a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for: the birth of a child and to care for the newborn; the placement of a child for adoption or foster care; the employee's own serious health condition; caring for the employee's spouse, child, or parent who has a serious health condition; or a qualifying exigency arising out of a covered military member's active-duty status. A separate, longer entitlement of up to 26 workweeks in a single 12-month period is available to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness. FMLA leave is unpaid by default, though an employee may substitute, or an employer may require the substitution of, the employee's own accrued paid leave

Synset.dc:source: 29 U.S.C. § 2611(4); 29 CFR § 825.104(a); federal-agency coverage split at 29 CFR § 825.109
Synset.Definition: An employer subject to the FMLA's leave and health-benefits obligations. In the private sector, a covered employer is a person engaged in commerce or in an industry or activity affecting commerce who employs 50 or more employees for each working day during each of 20 or more calendar workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. Public agencies are covered employers regardless of the number of employees they employ, as are both public and private elementary and secondary schools. Most ordinary federal civilian executive-branch employees are instead governed by a separate statutory leave scheme at 5 U.S.C. §§ 6381-6387 (so-called "Title II FMLA"), administered by the Office of Personnel Management rather than the Department of Labor; certain federal employers and employee categories -- including the Government Accountability Office, the Library of Congress, the U.S. Postal Service, the Postal Regulatory Commission, and some part-time or intermittent federal employees -- remain covered by this Title I definition instead

Under the FMLA, a "serious health condition" is an illness, injury, impairment, or physical or mental condition that involves inpatient care in a hospital, hospice, or residential medical care facility, or continuing treatment by a health care provider

The Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA) is a federal law whose purposes are to encourage noncareer service in the uniformed services by eliminating or minimizing the disadvantages to civilian careers and employment which can result from such service; to minimize the disruption to the lives of persons performing service in the uniformed services, as well as to their employers, their fellow employees, and their communities, by providing for the prompt reemployment of such persons upon their completion of such service; and to prohibit discrimination against persons because of their service in the uniformed services

An employee is eligible for FMLA leave only if all three conditions are met: the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months (the 12 months need not be consecutive, though employment periods before a break in service of 7 years or more generally do not count toward that 12-month total, subject to exceptions for a break caused by fulfilling USERRA-covered military service obligations or a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee); the employee has been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the start of the leave; and the employee works at a worksite where the employer employs at least 50 employees within 75 miles of that worksite

Synset.dc:source: 29 U.S.C. § 2612(c), (d); 29 CFR § 825.207; federal Paid Parental Leave track at 5 U.S.C. § 6382(d)(2)(B)(i), Pub. L. 116-92, div. F, tit. LXXVI, § 7602
Synset.Definition: FMLA leave under 29 U.S.C. Chapter 28 (Title I FMLA, covering private-sector, State/local-government, and covered-school employers) is unpaid by default: leave granted under the Act may consist of unpaid leave, except to the extent an employee substitutes, or an employer requires the substitution of, the employee's own accrued paid leave (vacation, personal, sick, or medical leave, as applicable to the reason for the FMLA leave) to run concurrently with the unpaid FMLA leave -- and other than a now-expired public-health-emergency leave category that applied only through December 31, 2020. Substitution rights are bounded by the terms of the employer's normal paid-leave policy, and paid leave taken for a non-FMLA-qualifying reason does not count against the employee's FMLA entitlement. This unpaid-by-default rule is specific to Title I FMLA and does not describe federal civilian employees' separate Title 5 FMLA leave, where, for births or placements occurring on or after October 1, 2020, birth/placement leave may be substituted with up to 12 administrative workweeks of Paid Parental Leave under the Federal Employee Paid Leave Act -- a separate statutory track that should not be cited for a private-sector employee's leave

An umbrella term for the FMLA's two distinct military-family-connected leave entitlements, which share a common statutory home, 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a), but differ sharply in length, triggering fact, and beneficiary class: qualifying exigency leave, capped at 12 workweeks and triggered by a covered military member's active-duty status itself, with no injury or illness required; and military caregiver leave, capped at 26 workweeks in a single 12-month period and triggered instead by a covered servicemember's serious injury or illness. The two are not additive: during a single 12-month period in which military caregiver leave is used, the aggregate entitlement is a combined total of 26 workweeks of leave covering both military caregiver leave and any other FMLA-qualifying reason, including qualifying exigency leave, used in that same period

FMLA leave because of a qualifying exigency arising out of the fact that the employee's spouse, or a son, daughter, or parent of the employee, is on covered active duty, or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty, in the Armed Forces. This leave falls within the FMLA's standard 12-workweek entitlement -- the same 12-workweek cap, during any 12-month period, that covers the Act's other standard leave reasons -- and is NOT the separate, longer 26-workweek military caregiver leave entitlement, which is triggered by a covered servicemember's serious injury or illness rather than by active-duty status alone. Nine categories of qualifying exigency are recognized by regulation: short-notice deployment; military events and related activities; childcare and school activities; financial and legal arrangements; counseling; rest and recuperation; post-deployment activities; parental care, for the military member's parent who is incapable of self-care; and additional activities agreed to by the employer and employee

Synset.dc:source: 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(3), (a)(4); "next of kin" priority order at 29 CFR § 825.127(d)(3)
Synset.Definition: FMLA leave to care for a covered servicemember who has a serious injury or illness, available to an eligible employee who is the spouse, son, daughter, parent, or next of kin of the servicemember, for up to 26 workweeks of leave during a single 12-month period -- the FMLA's longest leave entitlement, more than double the Act's standard 12-workweek cap. It is triggered by the servicemember's serious injury or illness, not by active-duty status alone, which distinguishes it from qualifying exigency leave, a different, 12-workweek entitlement triggered by active-duty status itself. During that single 12-month period the 26-workweek figure is a combined cap covering both this leave and any other FMLA-qualifying reason: an employee may use up to 12 of the 26 weeks for another FMLA-qualifying reason, including qualifying exigency leave, and up to 26 weeks total for military caregiver leave itself, but the two entitlements do not stack additively beyond 26 combined weeks. "Next of kin" here is itself a defined, sibling-inclusive term: the servicemember's nearest blood relative other than the spouse, parent, son, or daughter -- meaning a brother or sister shares a priority tier with grandparents, aunts, uncles, and first cousins, and, absent the servicemember's written designation of a specific relative, all relatives at the same priority tier (for example, multiple siblings) qualify simultaneously and may each take this leave -- so a sibling caregiver who does not qualify under the FMLA's general family-member definition can still qualify for leave specifically under this military-caregiver entitlement if the injured or ill family member is a covered servicemember

Synset.dc:source: 29 U.S.C. § 2611(7), (12), (13), § 2612(a)(1)(C); 29 CFR § 825.122(c), (d)(3); in loco parentis's disjunctive day-to-day-care-or-financial-support standard per DOL Administrator's Interpretation No. 2010-3 (convergence-tier: independently corroborated via two secondary legal-analysis sources quoting the interpretation's operative sentence verbatim, after dol.gov itself returned HTTP 403 to direct automated fetch of the primary document)
Synset.Definition: For purposes of FMLA leave to care for a family member with a serious health condition, "family member" is a closed, exhaustive list of exactly three relationship categories: the employee's spouse, the employee's son or daughter ("child"), and the employee's parent. This list does not include, and has no separate category for, a sibling (a brother or sister is not a covered family member under this particular leave entitlement), grandparent, grandchild, in-law, aunt, uncle, cousin, or unmarried domestic partner. The one narrow exception is functional, not relational: under the in loco parentis doctrine, an individual of any relationship, including a sibling, who has day-to-day responsibility to care for, or who financially supports, another person in a parental role can cause the cared-for person to legally qualify as the caregiving individual's "son or daughter" (if under 18, or 18 or older and incapable of self-care because of a mental or physical disability) or cause the caregiver to qualify as that person's "parent"; a biological or legal relationship is not required. DOL's own binding sub-regulatory guidance clarifies that day-to-day care and financial support are independently sufficient, not both required: an employee who intends to assume parental responsibility for someone need not show both providing day-to-day care AND providing financial support to stand in loco parentis -- either one alone can qualify. Ordinary adult sibling caregiving, without an underlying parent-child-type relationship established this way, does not by itself meet this standard. Separately, a sibling who does not qualify under this family-member definition may still qualify for the FMLA's distinct, longer military caregiver leave entitlement if the family member is a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, since that entitlement's own "next of kin" category is sibling-inclusive

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 409.31; CMS Pub. 100-02 (Medicare Benefit Policy Manual) Ch. 8 §30
Synset.Definition: SNF care is covered only if the patient requires skilled nursing or skilled rehabilitation services, ordered by a physician, for a condition treated during the qualifying hospital stay (or a condition that arose in the SNF for that same condition); the skilled services are needed on a daily basis; as a practical matter those daily skilled services can be provided only on an inpatient basis in a SNF; and the services are reasonable and necessary for treatment of the illness or injury

A service that must be ordered by a physician, requires the skills of qualified technical or professional personnel to be furnished safely and effectively, and must be furnished directly by or under the general supervision of such personnel; skilled nursing or rehabilitation care may be needed to improve a patient's condition, to maintain it, or to prevent or slow further deterioration — restoration potential is not the deciding factor

Skilled nursing and/or skilled rehabilitation services must be needed and provided on essentially a 7-day-a-week basis; where the stay rests solely on skilled rehabilitation services, the daily-basis requirement is satisfied by services needed and provided at least 5 days a week when 7-day availability is not feasible

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 411.15(g) (exclusion); 42 CFR 409.33 (examples of skilled services and personal-care-services list, establishing the skilled/custodial contrast implicitly rather than defining "custodial care" by name); CMS Pub. 100-02 Ch. 8 §30.5
Synset.Definition: Care that does not require the skills of technical or professional personnel and therefore does not meet the SNF level-of-care requirement — including administration of routine oral medications, general maintenance care of a colostomy or ileostomy, routine indwelling catheter care, routine incontinence care, and assistance with dressing, eating, and toileting; excluded from Medicare payment except as necessary for the palliation or management of terminal illness under the hospice benefit

The requirement that a beneficiary have been an inpatient of a participating hospital or critical access hospital, for medically necessary inpatient care, for at least 3 consecutive calendar days, not counting the date of discharge, before post-hospital SNF extended care services are coverable

Formal inpatient status of a hospital patient, which begins with the calendar day of admission as an inpatient under a physician's order; inpatient status is distinct from outpatient observation status, regardless of the patient's physical location or length of stay in the hospital

Hospital outpatient services furnished to evaluate a patient's condition or to determine the need for inpatient admission; time spent in observation status, or in the emergency room prior to or in lieu of an inpatient admission, does not count toward the 3-consecutive-day qualifying hospital stay requirement for SNF coverage

A period of consecutive days during which Medicare Part A benefits, subject to specified maximums, are available to a beneficiary; it begins the day the beneficiary first receives inpatient hospital, inpatient critical access hospital, or SNF services after becoming entitled to hospital insurance, and ends once the beneficiary has gone 60 consecutive days without being an inpatient of a hospital or SNF, at which point a new benefit period begins with fully renewed limits — also called a spell of illness

A benefit period ends when a beneficiary has, for at least 60 consecutive days, not been an inpatient of a hospital, a critical access hospital, or a skilled nursing facility; for this purpose a beneficiary counts as a SNF inpatient only for days that met the skilled level-of-care requirement, so non-skilled custodial SNF days do not extend the benefit period

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1395d(a)(2)(A) (100-day limit); 42 USC 1395e(a)(3) (days 21-100 coinsurance); 42 CFR 409.61; CMS Pub. 100-02 Ch. 3 §20.B
Synset.Definition: A beneficiary is entitled to have payment made for up to 100 days of covered posthospital extended care services in each benefit period; the first 20 days are covered in full, and days 21 through 100 are subject to daily coinsurance

Up to 90 days of inpatient hospital or critical access hospital coverage are available per benefit period — 60 full days plus 30 coinsurance days — plus a non-renewable lifetime reserve of 60 additional days usable across benefit periods once the 90 regular days are exhausted

Beyond the qualifying hospital stay, a beneficiary must also be admitted to a participating SNF and begin requiring or receiving covered-level care within 30 calendar days after hospital discharge, unless a medical-appropriateness exception applies

Synset.dc:source: CMS Pub. 100-02 (Medicare Benefit Policy Manual) Ch. 8 §20.2.3
Synset.Definition: If a beneficiary who is receiving covered post-hospital extended care leaves a SNF and is readmitted to the same or any other participating SNF for further covered care within 30 days after the day of discharge, the 30-day transfer requirement is considered met and no new qualifying hospital stay is required

A standardized notice that a Medicare provider — a skilled nursing facility, home health agency, comprehensive outpatient rehabilitation facility, or hospice — or a Medicare Advantage plan must deliver to a beneficiary before Medicare-covered skilled services end, explaining how to request an expedited review of the coverage termination; it notifies the beneficiary that Medicare coverage of the current course of treatment is ending and is not itself a notice of discharge or eviction from the facility

The transfer or discharge of a nursing facility resident against the resident's wishes, permitted only where necessary for the resident's welfare and the resident's needs cannot be met in the facility; where the resident's health has improved sufficiently that the facility's services are no longer needed; where the safety or health of other individuals in the facility is endangered; for nonpayment after reasonable and appropriate notice; or because the facility ceases to operate

The written notice a nursing facility must give before transferring or discharging a resident, generally at least 30 days in advance (with exceptions permitting notice as soon as practicable for safety, health, sufficient-improvement, or short-stay circumstances), delivered to the resident and the resident's representative with a copy to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman, stating the reason for the move, the effective date, the destination, and the resident's appeal rights

A resident who believes a nursing facility has erroneously determined that the resident must be transferred or discharged is entitled to a state fair hearing; once the resident invokes the right to appeal, the facility may not carry out the transfer or discharge while the appeal is pending unless the facility documents that failing to do so would endanger the health or safety of the resident or others in the facility

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 440.167(b); 42 CFR 441.450(c); CMS, Application for a §1915(c) Home and Community-Based Waiver: Instructions, Technical Guide and Review Criteria, Version 3.6 (Jan. 2019), pp. 119-120 (definitional source)
Synset.Definition: A person who has a duty under State law to care for another Medicaid beneficiary — customarily the beneficiary's spouse, or the parent (biological, adoptive, or step) of a minor child beneficiary; not customarily extended to the parent of an adult beneficiary (even one who also serves as legal guardian) or to other relative types, absent contrary State law. For purposes of the State Plan personal care services benefit, "family member" — the class of provider a beneficiary's personal care services may not be furnished by — means a legally responsible relative. The §1915(j) self-directed personal assistance services rules use the parallel, separately codified term "legally liable relative," defined as persons who have a duty under the provisions of State law to care for another person; under §1915(j) self-direction a State may elect to let a participant choose, as a paid provider, any individual capable of providing the assigned tasks, including a legally liable relative (42 USC 1396n(j)(4)(B)(i), permitting but not itself defining the term)

Synset.dc:source: CMS, Application for a §1915(c) Home and Community-Based Waiver: Instructions, Technical Guide and Review Criteria, Version 3.6 (Jan. 2019), pp. 108-110, Appendix C-2-d
Synset.Definition: Through a §1915(c) home and community-based services waiver, a State may elect to pay a legally responsible individual for personal-care-or-similar waiver services when the services constitute "extraordinary care" — care exceeding the range of activities that a legally responsible individual would ordinarily perform in the household on behalf of a person without a disability or chronic illness of the same age, and which are necessary to assure the health and welfare of the participant and avoid institutionalization; the State must specify in its approved waiver application the criteria it uses to distinguish extraordinary from ordinary care, together with best-interest safeguards, monitoring, and payment controls. This is a sub-regulatory CMS guidance standard, not a codified regulatory or statutory test

The opportunity for participants or their representatives to exercise choice and control over the budget, planning, and purchase of self-directed personal assistance services, including the amount, duration, scope, provider, and location of service provision, with participant decision-making authority that includes recruiting, hiring and discharging, scheduling, and supervising workers; under the Community First Choice rule, a consumer controlled method of selecting and providing services and supports that allows the individual maximum control, with the individual acting as the employer of record or having a significant and meaningful role in the management of an agency provider

Under §1915(i) State Plan home and community-based services self-direction, the authority a participant (or representative) exercises to select, manage, or dismiss providers of State plan HCBS, with the person-centered service plan specifying that authority, any limits on it, and which parties are responsible for functions outside the authority the individual exercises

Under §1915(i) State Plan home and community-based services self-direction, the authority a participant (or representative) exercises over an individualized service budget, including the plan's description of how the budget amount is calculated, the circumstances under which it may be adjusted, and the procedures for evaluating expenditures

Synset.dc:source: CMS §1915(c) Technical Guide v3.6 pp. 119-120 (defining "employer of record"); 42 CFR 441.450(a)-(c) (underlying self-direction authority); 42 CFR 441.505
Synset.Definition: Under Medicaid self-direction, the status of the participant (rather than a provider agency) acting as the common-law employer of the workers who furnish the participant's services — recruiting, hiring, discharging, scheduling, and supervising those workers — regardless of which entity performs payroll and tax functions on the participant's behalf; a Community First Choice self-directed-model participant may act as the employer of record or have a significant and meaningful role in the management of an agency provider

The §1915(k) Community First Choice State Plan option, covering home and community-based attendant services and supports for individuals meeting an institutional level-of-care standard, selected, managed, and dismissed by the individual (or representative) with maximum individual control regardless of who may act as the employer of record; attendant services may be provided by an individual who is qualified to provide such services, including family members (as defined by the Secretary), and under the self-directed model an individual has the option to permit family members, or any other individuals, to provide Community First Choice services and supports identified in the person-centered service plan, provided they meet the qualifications the individual has established

Under Medicaid self-direction, a person authorized to exercise self-direction decision-making on behalf of a participant who is unable to fully direct the participant's own services — for example, a minor child's parent or guardian, or another individual recognized by State law to act on behalf of an incapacitated adult; a person acting as a participant's representative is prohibited from also acting as a provider of self-directed services to that same participant. "Employer" or "employer authority" in the self-direction context is not a separate role held by some third party: every employer-authority provision assigns that authority to the participant, or to the participant's authorized representative acting on the participant's behalf, never to anyone else, so an authorized representative exercising employer authority IS the employer for that purpose, not someone distinct from it — a structural inference across the cited provisions, not a single directly-quotable holding; California's own Self-Determination Program materials illustrate the same pattern (a Department of Developmental Services financial-management-services comparison identifies the participant, extended by statute to the authorized representative "when appropriate," as the employer under every service model it offers)

Unpaid supports that are provided voluntarily to an individual in lieu of §1915(c) home and community-based waiver services and supports — for example, assistance from family, friends, or others given without payment; a person-centered service plan must reflect both paid and unpaid services and supports, including natural supports, and their providers

Synset.dc:source: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 4685.8(a), (c)(5); 42 USC § 1396n(c); CMS/Medicaid.gov, HCBS Waiver CA.1166.R01.00 ("CA Self-Determination Program for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities")
Synset.Definition: California's voluntary, statewide alternative to regional-center-directed services within the Lanterman Act developmental-services system: an eligible regional-center consumer -- or, when appropriate, the consumer's parent, legal guardian or conservator, or authorized representative -- plans, arranges, and directs an individually tailored array of services and supports within a fixed individual budget, through a person-centered planning process supported by an independent facilitator and financial management services, rather than having the regional center authorize services; a participant may leave the program at any time to resume traditional regional-center-authorized services. The program operates under its own, freestanding federal Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services waiver (CMS/DDS waiver control number CA.1166.R01.00), approved by CMS in 2018 as a capped pilot and implemented statewide for all eligible consumers effective July 1, 2021 -- a distinct waiver from California's original developmental-disabilities waiver (CA.0336.R05.00), and not a Community First Choice (§1915(k)) program

Under California's Self-Determination Program, the amount of regional center purchase-of-service funding available to a participant for the services and supports necessary to implement the participant's individual program plan, calculated by a fair, equitable, and transparent statutory methodology rather than by ordinary regional-center service authorization: for a current regional-center consumer entering the program, the initial individual budget equals the total of the consumer's most recent twelve months of purchase-of-service authorizations, plus any services the IPP team has already authorized but not yet formally placed in a purchase-of-service authorization, less services the regional center pays for outside the Self-Determination Program and one-time expenses; for a consumer new to, or without twelve months of history in, the regional-center system, the IPP team identifies the needed services and the regional center calculates the budget from the average cost the regional center pays for each identified service or support, which the regional center may adjust either higher or lower where it determines the participant has a documented unique need; budgets are subject to periodic recalculation as circumstances change. The individual budget is a ceiling on available funding, not itself an itemized plan of expenditures -- for the itemized allocation of that ceiling, see the spending plan. A participant may use Self-Determination Program funds only when generic services and supports are not available, so a participant who is also an In-Home Supportive Services recipient must use that generic resource for an overlapping need before using individual-budget funds for it; the individual budget itself remains administered separately from, and is never merged into, an In-Home Supportive Services hours/budget allocation

Under California's Self-Determination Program, the plan a participant develops to use the participant's available individual-budget funds to purchase the goods, services, and supports necessary to implement the participant's individual program plan, itemizing and identifying the cost of each good, service, and support to be purchased with regional-center funds. The spending plan is a distinct artifact from the individual budget: the individual budget is the dollar ceiling of available regional-center purchase-of-service funding, while the spending plan is the itemized document allocating that ceiling to specific purchases, and it cannot exceed the individual budget it draws against

Synset.dc:source: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 12300-12317.2, 4685.8(d)(3)(B); 42 CFR § 440.167; California Dept. of Developmental Services, Self-Determination Program FAQ
Synset.Definition: The monthly hours (and corresponding county payment amount) an In-Home Supportive Services recipient is authorized to receive, determined through an in-home needs assessment performed by a county social worker under the Functional Index ranking system, subject to statutory maximum-hours limits; administered by county welfare departments under the California Department of Social Services -- not by a regional center or the Department of Developmental Services -- and funded principally as an optional Medicaid State Plan personal-care benefit rather than under a §1915(c) Home and Community-Based Services waiver. California's own Self-Determination Program guidance describes In-Home Supportive Services as a "generic resource" that is not paid for through, or included in, the Self-Determination Program: a Self-Determination Program participant who is also an In-Home Supportive Services recipient must use In-Home Supportive Services for an overlapping need before Self-Determination individual-budget funds may be used for it, and the two allocations -- one a rank-based Functional Index hours calculation, the other a historically-anchored, IPP-team-negotiated dollar figure -- are administered by separate agencies under separate statutes and are never merged

Synset.dc:source: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code §§ 12300, 4685.8(d)(3)(B); 42 CFR § 440.167; 42 USC § 1396n(k); California Dept. of Developmental Services, Self-Determination Program FAQ
Synset.Definition: California's statewide, county-administered Medi-Cal program that pays for in-home domestic and personal-care services -- housework, meal preparation, bathing, dressing, ambulation, accompaniment, protective supervision, and related paramedical tasks -- for aged, blind, or disabled state residents who cannot safely remain in their own homes without such assistance. Structured as an optional Medicaid State Plan personal-care benefit, funded in part through the Community First Choice Option (§1915(k), since 2011, carrying an enhanced federal matching rate) layered onto that core authority, rather than delivered as a Home and Community-Based Services waiver, and delivered through county welfare/social-services departments under the California Department of Social Services rather than through a licensed home health agency or a regional center. A California regional-center consumer eligible for the Self-Determination Program may simultaneously be an In-Home Supportive Services recipient, but the two programs are administered by different state departments under different statutory schemes, and a Self-Determination Program participant must use In-Home Supportive Services -- a "generic resource" under California Dept. of Developmental Services guidance -- for an overlapping need before using Self-Determination individual-budget funds for it

Synset.dc:source: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 12300.1; Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 2725, 2727; Cal. Dept. of Social Services, Functional Index Rankings and Hourly Task Guidelines (Nov. 2020)
Synset.Definition: A category of skilled or paramedical-adjacent personal-care tasks -- for example medication administration and injections, blood or urine testing, wound care, catheter or ostomy care, tube feeding, suctioning, and other sterile-procedure or judgment-requiring tasks -- that a recipient could perform for themselves but for functional limitation, and that a self-directed in-home-care worker may perform only pursuant to a licensed health care professional's order, direction, and hands-on training, and only with the recipient's informed consent. California's In-Home Supportive Services statute does not use the phrase "Health Maintenance Activities" -- its own term of art for this category is "paramedical services," ordered by a licensed health care professional, rendered under that professional's direction, subject to the recipient's informed consent; "Health Maintenance Activities"/"HMA" is the parallel term of art used in other states' analogous self-directed personal-care programs for the same broad category of delegated skilled tasks. Because the licensed professional retains the ordering clinical judgment and the worker only executes under that direction and the recipient's informed consent, delegating a paramedical task does not itself convert the worker into a licensed nurse or the program into a nursing program, consistent with the exemption for a person who carries out a licensed professional's orders without holding out as practicing as a professional nurse -- a synthesis of these provisions, not a single directly-quotable holding. California's IHSS Functional Index ranks most service categories (housework, meal preparation, bathing, transfers, feeding, among others) on a graduated scale reflected in a standardized Hourly Task Guidelines table; paramedical services sit outside that standardized grid -- the Functional Index Rankings document lists "Requires Paramedical Services, prescribed by a licensed health care professional" as its own top rank, but paramedical hours are authorized individually according to the treating licensed health care professional's specific order and frequency, not drawn from the standardized hourly-task grid the way other service categories are. Because each service category is independently assessed, needing paramedical/Health-Maintenance-Activities-type assistance for one task does not itself convert a recipient's independently-assessed needs in other categories into paramedical services -- a structural inference from the Functional Index's per-category design, not a directly-quotable rule

A home-health-agency-delivered, physician-ordered skilled nursing and therapy benefit -- distinct from the personal-care/attendant-care model of In-Home Supportive Services and similar self-directed programs. In California, an organization that provides, or arranges for the provision of, skilled nursing services in a person's place of residence must be licensed as a home health agency; "skilled nursing services" means services provided by a registered nurse or licensed vocational nurse. This licensed-home-health-agency model is the medical-model California analog of what other states' Medicaid guidance materials label "Long-Term Home Health (LTHH)" -- a federal Medicaid "home health care services" concept, distinct there from "personal care services." "LTHH" is not itself a defined California statutory or regulatory term, nor a federal Medicaid regulatory term of art located in this research; it is a term used, for example, in Colorado's state Medicaid guidance for its own home-health-agency benefit, and should not be treated as a citable California program name absent further verification

Synset.dc:source: NASHP, Medicaid Structured Family Caregiving: Enabling Family Members to Make Caregiving Their Primary Focus (Aug. 2022)
Synset.Definition: A named service model used in some States' §1915(c) home and community-based services waivers — distinct from hourly personal-care or attendant-care billing — in which a live-in caregiver, often a family member, receives a flat daily stipend from a licensed provider agency for making caregiving the caregiver's primary occupation, with agency-supplied training, coaching, monitoring, and respite backup; there is no federal "Structured Family Caregiving" benefit category, and its availability, eligibility, and stipend amount vary by State and by waiver. As of 2022, documented in Connecticut, Georgia, Indiana, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina, and South Dakota, each under its own §1915(c) waiver(s)

Synset.dc:source: Mont. Code Ann. § 37-2-603; Montana DPHHS, Pediatric Complex Care Assistant Services
Synset.Definition: A Montana Medicaid State Plan service, not a waiver service, under which a trained parent, guardian, other family member, or kinship or foster care provider may be paid to deliver physician-ordered care to a Montana Healthcare Programs member under age 21 with medically complex needs; PCCA services complement, rather than replace, other Medicaid services such as private duty nursing and personal care services, and Montana was the first State to offer this service under a Medicaid State Plan. A State-specific illustration of the same paid-family-caregiving-for-a-medically-complex-child policy problem the §1915(c) extraordinary care exception addresses, but authorized under Montana's own State law and State Plan rather than CMS's 1915(c) extraordinary-care guidance

Synset.dc:source: IRC § 3504; IRS Revenue Procedure 70-6; IRS Notice 2003-70
Synset.Definition: An entity operating as agent for a Medicaid self-direction participant under section 3504 of the Internal Revenue Code, designated to file certain federal, State, and local employment tax returns and pay applicable withholding, FICA, and FUTA taxes on the participant's behalf as common-law employer, functioning as one of the financial management entity models used to process worker payroll for participant-directed personal assistance services

Synset.dc:source: Minn. Stat. § 256B.85; Minnesota Dept. of Human Services, Community First Services and Supports
Synset.Definition: Minnesota's Medicaid program combining the federal §1915(k) Community First Choice option and the §1915(i) State Plan home and community-based services option into a single participant-controlled service, replacing Minnesota's prior Personal Care Assistance and Consumer Support Grant programs effective October 1, 2024; a State-specific illustration of the federal Community First Choice option, not itself a distinct federal authority

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006) §§ 102(7), 109(a); Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) § 301(a)
Synset.Definition: A writing or other record by which an individual (the principal) grants authority to another person (the agent) to act in the principal's place, whether or not the document itself uses the phrase "power of attorney"; the power is effective when executed unless the instrument itself provides for a future effective date or contingency. A power of attorney is a private appointment instrument the principal executes without any court proceeding -- categorically distinct from a guardianship, under which a court adjudicates the respondent's inability to meet essential needs (not a status of "incapacity" -- the 2017 Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act deliberately moved away from that term) through a petition, notice, and hearing, and appoints a substitute decision-maker by judicial order

A power of attorney that is not terminated by the principal's later incapacity -- one that continues in effect even after the principal can no longer supervise or ratify the agent's acts. Under the Uniform Power of Attorney Act's default rule, a power of attorney created under the Act is durable unless the instrument expressly provides that the principal's incapacity terminates it, reversing the older common-law default under which an ordinary agency terminated automatically on the principal's incapacity

A power of attorney that is not durable: one that terminates automatically, by operation of law, the moment the principal becomes incapacitated, rather than continuing through the principal's incapacity as a durable power of attorney does by statutory default

A power of attorney that does not take effect immediately upon execution but instead becomes effective only upon a future date or the occurrence of a specified future event or contingency -- most commonly a determination that the principal has become incapacitated -- as opposed to a power of attorney effective immediately upon signing. Where effectiveness is conditioned on incapacity and the instrument names no one to determine that the contingency has occurred, the power springs into effect upon a written determination: by a physician or licensed psychologist for incapacity based on the principal's impairment, or by an attorney at law, a judge, or an appropriate governmental official for incapacity based on the principal's unavailability -- the Act treats these as two textually distinct determination pathways, not interchangeable alternatives for the same kind of incapacity. "Springing" is standard practitioner and treatise terminology for this mechanism; the word does not appear in the Act's own operative numbered subsections, which instead codify the mechanism directly as a delayed-effectiveness condition, though the Act's accompanying Official Comment to §109 does use "springing" repeatedly as the mechanism's common name

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006) §§ 102(7), 103(2), 201(a), (c), 204, 208, 216 (real-property, banking, and tax authority bundles); Cal. Prob. Code § 4265 (will non-delegability)
Synset.Definition: A power of attorney granting an agent authority over the principal's property, business, and financial affairs, as opposed to health-care decisions, which the Uniform Power of Attorney Act expressly excludes from its own scope. A grant of "general authority" as to a named subject (e.g., real property, banks and financial institutions, taxes) incorporates a statutorily-enumerated bundle of specific powers for that subject unless the instrument narrows or excludes them -- general real-property authority lets the agent buy, sell, lease, mortgage, and otherwise deal with real property; general banking authority lets the agent open and close accounts, borrow money, and negotiate commercial paper; general tax authority lets the agent prepare and file returns and contest deficiencies. A short list of especially consequential acts -- making gifts, creating or amending a trust, changing beneficiary designations, delegating authority -- requires an express, specific grant and is never included merely by granting "general" authority. Making, amending, or revoking the principal's will is categorically non-delegable; the Uniform Power of Attorney Act itself is silent on wills (the word "will" does not appear anywhere in its text in this sense), but California, for example, expressly bars a power of attorney from authorizing an agent to make, publish, declare, amend, or revoke the principal's will

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (1993) §§ 1(2), (12)-(13), 2(b)-(d); Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006) § 103(2); 42 USC 1395cc(f)(3); 42 USC 1396a(w)(4); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2980
Synset.Definition: A written legal instrument, executed by a competent adult (the principal), that designates another person (the agent) with authority to make health-care decisions on the principal's behalf. Unless the instrument specifies otherwise, the agent's authority is dormant until a determination that the principal lacks capacity, made -- absent contrary instructions -- by the principal's "primary physician," a deliberate term choice by the Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act's drafters, who avoided "attending physician" as ambiguous between any treating physician and the one with primary responsibility for the individual's care. It is a legally distinct instrument from a financial/durable power of attorney: the Uniform Power of Attorney Act expressly excludes "a power to make health-care decisions" from its own scope. New York's parallel state-law term for this instrument is a "health care proxy," delegating authority to a "health care agent"

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1395cc(f)(3); 42 USC 1396a(w)(4); Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (1993) §§ 1(1), (9)
Synset.Definition: The federally-defined umbrella term for a written instruction relating to the provision of health care when the maker is later incapacitated -- such as a living will or a durable power of attorney for health care -- recognized under State law; Medicare and Medicaid providers must give written information on state-law rights to accept or refuse treatment and to formulate advance directives, document advance-directive status in the medical record, and not condition care on whether a beneficiary has executed one. Enacted as the Patient Self-Determination Act, sections 4206 and 4751 of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990, Pub. L. 101-508, 104 Stat. 1388. The Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act frames the identical concept as "an individual instruction or a power of attorney for health care"; its "individual instruction" component -- called a "living will" in the federal statute's own illustrative, but not independently statutorily-defined, phrasing -- is a direct statement of the individual's own treatment preferences, as opposed to the appointment of a decision-making agent

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006) § 102(9); Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (1993) §§ 1(2), (12)
Synset.Definition: An individual who grants authority to an agent in a power of attorney; the same "individual granting the power" role recurs in the health-care context under the Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act, which uses that phrase to identify the principal's role without formally defining the word "principal" itself as a standalone term

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Power of Attorney Act (2006) § 102(1); Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (1993) § 1(2); N.Y. Public Health Law § 2980; CMS, Application for a §1915(c) Home and Community-Based Waiver: Instructions, Technical Guide and Review Criteria, Version 3.6 (Jan. 2019), pp. 119-120 (LRI-status distinction); 20 CFR §§ 404.2010, 416.601
Synset.Definition: A person granted authority by a principal to act on the principal's behalf under a power of attorney, whether the governing document calls the role "agent," "attorney-in-fact," or another label; the term includes an original agent, a coagent, a successor agent, and a person to whom an agent's authority has been further delegated. The identical role in the health-care context is a "health care agent" -- under New York's health care proxy statute, an adult to whom authority to make health care decisions is delegated under a health care proxy. Neither an agent's appointment under a power of attorney nor a court-appointed guardian's appointment automatically makes that person a Medicaid HCBS "legally responsible individual": LRI status turns on a family relationship (customarily a spouse, or the parent of a minor-child beneficiary; not customarily extended to the parent of an adult beneficiary), not on holding a POA or guardianship appointment. Nor does either appointment automatically make that person a Social Security representative payee -- the Social Security Administration independently determines incapability to manage benefit payments and selects a payee through its own administrative process, not by recognizing a POA

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) §§ 102(9), (12), 301(a)-(b); SSA POMS GN 00502.139; CMS, Application for a §1915(c) Home and Community-Based Waiver: Instructions, Technical Guide and Review Criteria, Version 3.6 (Jan. 2019), pp. 119-120 (LRI-status distinction)
Synset.Definition: A person appointed by a court to make decisions with respect to the personal (non-financial) affairs of another individual -- termed the "individual subject to guardianship" in the modern Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act's own vocabulary, which deliberately eliminated the older term "ward" as unnecessarily stigmatizing (still the operative term in some non-uniform-act States, e.g. Florida). Guardianship requires a court proceeding -- petition, notice, hearing, and a judicial finding by clear-and-convincing evidence that the individual lacks the ability to meet essential requirements for physical health, safety, or self-care and that no less restrictive alternative (including supported decision-making or an agent under a power of attorney) would meet those needs -- a categorically different appointment mechanism from a power of attorney, which the principal executes privately with no judicial finding required. Court appointment as guardian likewise does not automatically make a person the representative payee for the individual's Social Security or SSI benefit payments: the Social Security Administration independently selects a payee under its own process and "is not required to appoint the legal guardian as payee" -- it appoints whoever will best serve the beneficiary. Nor does guardianship of an adult automatically confer Medicaid HCBS "legally responsible individual" status, which is not customarily extended to a parent of an adult beneficiary even where that parent also serves as legal guardian

In States that have not adopted the guardian/conservator functional split of the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act, the sub-type of guardian authorized to act on a ward's person -- as opposed to the ward's property -- covering personal, health, and welfare decisions; Florida, for example, defines "guardian" as a person appointed to act on behalf of a ward's person or property, or both, with "guardian of the person" recurring in the operative text of Florida's guardian-powers statute (though not itself a section heading) for the personal-affairs track. In UGCOPAA States this same personal-affairs authority is simply called "guardian," with no separate "of the person" qualifier needed because UGCOPAA already assigns property/financial authority to an entirely separate office, "conservator"

In States that have not adopted the guardian/conservator functional split of the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act, the sub-type of guardian authorized to act on a ward's property and financial affairs -- as opposed to the ward's person. Pennsylvania, which has no "conservator" office at all, authorizes a court to appoint "a guardian or guardians of his person or estate" for an incapacitated person, with the estate track covering property management. Florida's parallel term is "guardian of the property," not "guardian of the estate" -- the word "estate" does not appear in Florida's guardian definitions; Florida instead distinguishes a ward's "person" from a ward's "property" throughout its guardianship chapter. In UGCOPAA States this same property-management function is called "conservator," not "guardian of the estate" or "guardian of the property" -- UGCOPAA does not use either phrase anywhere in its text

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) §§ 102(8), 301(b); Fla. Stat. § 744.102(9)(b)
Synset.Definition: A guardianship that grants the guardian all powers available under the governing guardianship statute. Under the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act, a court may not establish a full guardianship if a limited guardianship, a protective arrangement instead of guardianship, or another less restrictive alternative would meet the individual's needs -- full guardianship is legally disfavored, granted only when the individual's demonstrated needs require it. Florida's parallel term for the same concept is "plenary guardian": a person appointed to exercise all delegable legal rights and powers of the ward

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) §§ 102(16), 301(b); Fla. Stat. § 744.102(9)(a)
Synset.Definition: A guardianship that grants the guardian less than all powers available under the governing guardianship statute, or that otherwise restricts the guardian's powers. A court must grant a guardian only those powers necessitated by the individual's demonstrated needs and limitations, issuing orders that encourage the individual's maximum self-determination and independence -- the statutorily preferred default over full/plenary guardianship whenever it would meet the individual's needs. Florida's parallel term is "limited guardian": a guardian appointed to exercise only the legal rights and powers specifically designated by court order

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017), Official Comment to § 309; Wash. Rev. Code § 11.130.010(26); 755 ILCS 5/13-1.1, 5/13-1.2
Synset.Definition: A person or entity that serves as guardian (or conservator) as a paid occupation rather than as an unpaid family member or friend. The Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act does not itself define "professional guardian" -- the phrase appears only in non-operative official Comment text to § 309 cautioning that "courts should resist the temptation to appoint a professional guardian simply because it is difficult to choose among family members and friends," since it "comes at significant financial cost" to the individual. Licensure and certification are State-specific: Washington defines a "professional guardian or conservator" as one who is not a relative of the person under guardianship and who charges fees for serving three or more such persons, while Illinois requires public guardians appointed by the Governor (a narrower population than all Illinois public guardians -- the public guardian for a county over 1,000,000 in population is instead appointed by the chief judge of the circuit court and is not subject to this requirement) to hold National Certified Guardian certification from the Center for Guardianship Certification

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) § 312; 755 ILCS 5/11a-3.2
Synset.Definition: An expedited, time-limited grant of guardianship authority a court can put in place to prevent imminent harm before or without a full guardianship proceeding. Under the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act, a court may appoint an emergency guardian for an adult for up to 60 days (extendable once for up to another 60 days) on findings that appointment is likely to prevent substantial harm to the adult's physical health, safety, or welfare, that no one else has authority and willingness to act, and that there is reason to believe a basis for guardianship exists; the court must immediately appoint the respondent an attorney, and appointment without prior notice requires a further finding of imminent substantial harm, with notice due within 48 hours and a hearing within 5 days. Appointment of an emergency guardian is expressly not itself a determination that a basis for guardianship exists. A separate, non-court mechanism exists in some States for an adult already under guardianship: Illinois, for example, allows an existing guardian of a disabled adult to appoint, by signed writing with no additional court approval, a short-term guardian to take over the guardian's duties for up to 60 cumulative days in any 12-month period -- a genuinely different mechanism from the court-ordered emergency guardian despite the overlapping "short-term"/"temporary"/"emergency" vocabulary, and distinct from Illinois's separate, minor-only short-term-guardian statute, under which a parent (not an existing guardian) may appoint a short-term guardian for a child for up to 365 days

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) §§ 102(5), (9); Cal. Prob. Code §§ 1500, 1800, 1800.3(a), 1801(a)-(c); 20 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 5511
Synset.Definition: In a growing minority of U.S. States -- roughly a dozen that have enacted the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act or its 1997 predecessor -- a person appointed by a court to make decisions with respect to the property or financial affairs of an individual, the separate, property-focused counterpart office to "guardian" (personal affairs). California is a documented outlier: it has not adopted UGCOPAA, and instead uses "conservator" as the umbrella term for both the personal-care and financial-management roles for adults, reserving "guardian" for minors -- splitting the function internally instead, as "conservator of the person," "conservator of the estate," or "conservator of the person and estate," for the protected adult (the "conservatee"). Pennsylvania is a further variant: it has no "conservator" office at all, and covers the identical property-management function as a sub-type of guardian instead ("guardian... of... estate"). Because the term's scope inverts by jurisdiction -- non-overlapping with guardian in UGCOPAA States, an age-based rather than function-based split from guardian in California, and absent altogether in Pennsylvania -- no single cross-jurisdiction relationship between "conservator" and "guardian" holds universally

Synset.dc:source: Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act (2017) §§ 301(a)(1)-(b), 102(13) and Official Comment to § 301; Minn. Stat. § 524.5-102, subd. 6
Synset.Definition: The statutory threshold a court must find, by clear-and-convincing evidence, before appointing a guardian for an adult. The modern Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act deliberately does not define or use the term "incapacitated person" -- rejected, per its own drafting history, as "demeaning and even offensive" -- and instead requires a particularized, functional finding: that the individual lacks the ability to meet essential requirements for physical health, safety, or self-care because the individual is unable to receive and evaluate information or make or communicate decisions, even with appropriate supportive services, technological assistance, or supported decision-making, and that the individual's needs cannot be met by a less restrictive alternative (including supported decision-making or an agent under a power of attorney). The Act's own Comment to § 301 explains the shift: rather than assigning the individual a status such as "incapacitated" or "has capacity," the court makes particularized findings about what the individual can and cannot do. "Incapacitated person" survives as an operative defined term in States still on the older 1997 Uniform Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Act framework -- Minnesota, for example, defines it as an individual impaired to the extent of lacking sufficient understanding or capacity to make personal decisions and unable to meet personal needs for medical care, nutrition, clothing, shelter, or safety, even with appropriate assistance

A default, fallback hierarchy of family members and others who may make health-care decisions for an individual only in the absence of an affirmative appointment -- no valid, in-effect health care power of attorney or advance directive. A power of attorney is an affirmative act chosen by the principal that supersedes reliance on any later tier of the default hierarchy the moment it is validly executed and in effect, for the scope it grants. Florida's default surrogate-decision-maker priority order, illustrative of the pattern found in most States, runs: a judicially appointed guardian or guardian advocate, if one has been appointed with the relevant authority; then, if none has, spouse; adult child (or a majority of adult children reasonably available); parent; adult sibling (or a majority of siblings reasonably available); another adult relative who has exhibited special care and concern; a close friend; then a licensed clinical social worker selected through the facility's bioethics process -- each tier is skipped only if no one at that tier is reasonably available, willing, or competent to act
