A person or organization selected and appointed by the Social Security Administration (SSA) to receive Title II (Social Security) or Title XVI (SSI) benefit payments on behalf of a beneficiary SSA has determined is unable to manage or direct the management of those payments; every beneficiary otherwise retains the right to manage his or her own benefits, and payee appointment is an exception SSA makes only where it finds direct payment would not serve the beneficiary's interest. Representative-payee status is SSA's own independent administrative determination, made and filled under SSA's own regulatory criteria -- it is not conferred by, and does not require, a power of attorney or a court-appointed guardianship. A power of attorney makes no finding about the principal's capability or legal competence, and federal Treasury regulations bar a general or durable power of attorney from being used to negotiate a Social Security or SSI benefit check; an agent under a power of attorney who wants to manage a beneficiary's benefits must apply to SSA and be evaluated like any other candidate, the same rule that applies to a court-appointed guardian

The standard under which SSA directs benefit payments to a representative payee rather than to the beneficiary directly. For a beneficiary 18 years old or older, SSA pays a representative payee when it appears that doing so will be in the beneficiary's interest because the beneficiary is legally incompetent or mentally incapable of managing benefit payments, or physically incapable of managing or directing the management of those payments. For a beneficiary under 18, representative payment is the general rule, subject to enumerated exceptions under which direct payment may still be made; three of those exceptions are Title-II-specific (Social Security) and do not extend to Title XVI (SSI) minors -- a minor entitled on his or her own disability record, a minor in military service, or an emancipated or self-supporting minor -- while a minor parent with demonstrated money-management experience, a minor capable of using the benefits for current needs with no qualified payee available, or a minor within 7 months of turning 18 filing an initial claim are direct-payment exceptions under both Title II and Title XVI

SSA's stated, but flexible and non-mandatory, order of preference among candidates when it must select who will serve as a representative payee. For an adult beneficiary, the order generally starts with a legal guardian or a spouse or other relative with custody of, or demonstrated strong concern for, the beneficiary's welfare, continues through other qualified relatives and non-relative custodians, and ends with other suitable persons or qualified organizations; a separate track applies where the beneficiary's impairment is drug addiction or alcoholism, favoring a community-based nonprofit social service agency that is either licensed by the State or bonded; and a separate track applies for a minor beneficiary, beginning with a natural or adoptive parent with custody or a guardian and ending with an authorized social agency or custodial institution. SSA also considers any advance designation the beneficiary made of a preferred payee, ahead of applying the default order, where the designee is willing, able, and not disqualified

The affirmative, ongoing duties a representative payee owes the beneficiary and SSA: to use benefits received on the beneficiary's behalf only for the beneficiary's use and benefit; to keep any benefits received separate from the payee's own funds, with narrow exceptions, preserving the beneficiary's ownership interest including any interest earned; to notify SSA of any event or change in circumstances affecting the amount of, or the beneficiary's right to, benefits, or affecting the payee's own ability to serve; and to submit to SSA, upon request, a written report accounting for the benefits received, with supporting records made available

The standard defining what counts as spending benefits for the beneficiary's "use and benefit," elaborating the representative payee's duty to use benefits only for the beneficiary's own use: the costs of the beneficiary's current maintenance, meaning food, shelter, clothing, medical care, and personal comfort items, plus, for an institutionalized beneficiary, customary institutional charges and expenditures that aid the beneficiary's recovery or release (a Title-XVI/SSI beneficiary in an institution receiving over 50 percent Medicaid funding is held to a narrower rule instead: benefits may be used only for the beneficiary's own personal needs, not general institutional charges). Only under Title II (Social Security) may a payee, after current needs are met, use part of the payments for the support of the beneficiary's legally dependent spouse, child, or parent -- Title XVI (SSI) has no comparable dependent-support provision

SSA's requirement that a representative payee submit a written accounting of how benefits were used, in writing, at least once a year, with limited exemptions (for example, certain parents of minor beneficiaries and spouse-payees); SSA can require the payee (not the beneficiary) to receive the beneficiary's benefits in person at a local field office or designated government facility if the payee fails to file the required report. The CFR text itself uses "written report[ing]"/"accounting," not the phrase "representative payee report" -- that label is SSA administrative/POMS usage, carried in this lexicon only as a colloquial synonym, not as CFR-defined terminology

SSA alone terminates an existing representative-payee arrangement, selects a replacement, or converts a beneficiary to direct payment; the governing regulation is written entirely as SSA's own action, triggered by defined conditions such as misuse of benefits, the payee's non-compliance with its duties, the payee's death, resignation, or incapacity, or the payee's failure to cooperate with SSA's requests for evidence. A third party -- a nursing facility, a family member, the current payee, or the beneficiary -- cannot itself change the payee of record; it can only file an application (Form SSA-11, "Request to be Selected as Payee") or otherwise ask SSA to make the change, after which an SSA field office interviews the applicant and independently decides whether to make the appointment. Neither an existing power of attorney nor a court-appointed guardianship authorizes its holder to change the payee outside this SSA process

A representative payee who misuses a beneficiary's benefits is personally liable to repay the misused amount, which SSA treats as an overpayment to the payee, and SSA must make every reasonable effort to obtain restitution from the payee. SSA itself reissues the misused benefits to the beneficiary or a successor payee in two circumstances: automatically, where the misusing payee is an organization or an individual payee serving 15 or more beneficiaries; and, for an individual payee serving 14 or fewer beneficiaries, only where SSA's own "negligent failure" to investigate or monitor that payee caused the misuse -- including SSA's failure to investigate or monitor per established procedures, untimely investigation of reported misuse, or continuing payments after the misuse was discovered. The reissued amount equals the misused benefits minus any amount SSA already collected from the payee

A federal cash-assistance program under Title XVI of the Social Security Act, administered by SSA but legally and financially distinct from the Social Security insurance system: it pays a monthly benefit to an aged, blind, or disabled individual whose income and resources fall below prescribed limits, with eligibility turning on financial need rather than any history of Social-Security-covered work, and funded from general U.S. Treasury revenues rather than the Social Security trust funds; the amount of a recipient's income is a major factor in both SSI eligibility and the amount of the SSI benefit

A Title II social-insurance program that pays monthly cash benefits to a worker who is both insured for disability benefits -- has earned a sufficient number of quarters of coverage through Social-Security-taxed work -- and medically "under a disability": unable to engage in substantial gainful activity by reason of a medically determinable physical or mental impairment expected to result in death or to last at least 12 continuous months. Benefits are not payable until after a waiting period: the earliest period of five consecutive calendar months, beginning no earlier than the 17th month before the month of application, throughout which the individual has been under a disability; SSI has no comparable statutory waiting period, since SSI eligibility turns on current income and resources rather than a disability-duration gate. SSDI is funded by dedicated payroll taxes into the Social Security trust funds and paid without regard to financial need, unlike SSI, a needs-based program funded from general revenue; the Congressional Research Service's own terminology for this contrast is "social insurance" (SSDI) versus "public assistance" (SSI), with SSI eligibility described as "based on financial need" -- close in substance, but not the exact phrase, to SSA's own consumer materials calling SSI "needs-based"

A Title II social-insurance benefit paid to a fully insured worker who has reached at least age 62 and applied, calculated from the worker's own career earnings record (the primary insurance amount); as with SSDI, eligibility depends on insured status and work credits rather than financial need; like SSDI, the program is funded through payroll taxes deposited into a dedicated Social Security trust fund rather than general revenue

Title II insurance benefits paid to the surviving spouse, surviving divorced spouse, or child of a worker who died fully or currently insured: a child's insurance benefit for the child of an individual entitled to old-age or disability insurance benefits, or who died fully or currently insured, a widow's insurance benefit for the surviving wife or surviving divorced wife of an individual who died fully insured, and a parallel widower's insurance benefit for the surviving husband or surviving divorced husband of an individual who died fully insured. As with retirement benefits, eligibility flows from the deceased worker's insured status and earnings record, not the survivor's own financial need

Synset.dc:source: Indiana Medicaid (IHCP), Sandata Electronic Visit Verification (EVV): Visit Maintenance (visit-status and exception-clearing guidance), in.gov/medicaid/providers/files/Sandata-EVV-Visit-Maintenance.pdf
Synset.Definition: In an electronic visit verification system, a visit that contains no outstanding exceptions — its required visit data having been captured, corrected, or acknowledged — so that it is eligible to be matched to a submitted claim; a visit with unresolved exceptions cannot reach verified status

Synset.dc:source: Indiana Medicaid (IHCP), Sandata Electronic Visit Verification (EVV): Visit Maintenance (Key Terminology)
Synset.Definition: The module within an electronic visit verification system in which visits are corrected and/or acknowledged; it is needed because a visit carrying an exception (missing or noncompliant data) cannot be verified or matched to a claim until a user documents the missing or incorrect data or acknowledges the exception

Synset.dc:source: Indiana Medicaid (IHCP), Sandata Electronic Visit Verification (EVV): Visit Maintenance (Key Terminology)
Synset.Definition: In electronic visit verification visit maintenance, a value chosen from a predefined list that explains why a change is being made to a visit's data; a reason code must be selected whenever visit data is changed, and is entered together with a resolution code (which documents the action taken) to clear or acknowledge an exception

Synset.dc:source: Nebraska DHHS, Division of Medicaid & Long-Term Care, EVV Personal Care Services FAQ (Geofence Requirement), dhhs.ne.gov
Synset.Definition: In electronic visit verification, a GPS-based virtual perimeter around the scheduled service location, used to validate that a caregiver checks in and out where the service is authorized; a visit started or ended outside the perimeter fails location verification. The permitted distance from the scheduled location is the geofence radius, which a State may set — for example, Nebraska sets it by ZIP code at 0.50 miles for rural and 0.25 miles for urban designated ZIP codes

Synset.dc:source: HHAeXchange Knowledge Base, "What is the consecutive shifts feature?", knowledge.hhaexchange.com
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification feature that lets a caregiver record a single clock-in and clock-out covering multiple back-to-back shifts for the same client, or one consecutive shift serving two linked clients at the same address (for example spouses receiving successive services); the captured visit data is applied to each covered visit

Synset.dc:source: Ohio Department of Medicaid, OMES System User Training Guide (Late and Missed Visit Detail Report)
Synset.Definition: A scheduled electronic visit verification visit for which no clock-in (call-in) was ever received; it is distinguished from a late visit, where a clock-in was received but occurred after the scheduled start time

Synset.dc:source: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, FAQ-EVV (DHS Sandata), pa.gov
Synset.Definition: An electronic visit verification visit delivered at the point of care without a pre-existing matching schedule in the system; because no schedule is linked, the caregiver must manually select the service being provided when starting the visit

Synset.dc:source: Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, FAQ-EVV (General EVV); Missouri MO HealthNet, Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Soft Launch of Claims Validation
Synset.Definition: An initial electronic visit verification rollout period during which claims are validated against EVV visit data and monitored but are not denied for mismatches, giving provider agencies, caregivers, and clients time to adapt before enforcement (the "hard launch") begins and non-matching claims are denied

Synset.dc:source: Indiana Medicaid (IHCP), Sandata Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) System Overview
Synset.Definition: The provider-agency user account that manages an agency's electronic visit verification users and data; in the Sandata EVV portal the Agency EVV Security Administrator uses the agency's master credentials to create and manage all other agency EVV user accounts, assigning each staff member and caregiver a unique username, password, and role

Synset.dc:source: Michigan DHHS, Community Health Automated Medicaid Processing System (CHAMPS), michigan.gov/mdhhs
Synset.Definition: The Community Health Automated Medicaid Processing System — the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services' web-based, rules-driven, real-time Medicaid management system, comprising provider enrollment, eligibility and enrollment, prior authorization, claims and encounters, and contracts management; Michigan Medicaid providers use it to enroll, update information, submit and adjust claims, verify eligibility, and check payment status

Synset.dc:source: Consumer Direct Care Network (CareAttend); Consumer Direct Care Network Washington (Terms and Definitions; mileage submission)
Synset.Definition: The Consumer Direct Care Network mobile electronic visit verification application used in self-directed care programs; care attendants use it on a mobile device to clock in and out and submit their time, satisfying the EVV clock-in/clock-out requirement of the 21st Century Cures Act. In Washington's CDWA program it is used only for time entry — mileage is submitted separately through the DirectMyCare web portal or the IVR system, not through CareAttend

Synset.dc:source: HHAeXchange Knowledge Base, Signature Report, knowledge.hhaexchange.com
Synset.Definition: In an electronic visit verification system, a report that lets an agency review captured patient (member) signatures for visits — showing details such as visit date, patient, contract, caregiver, and scheduled/confirmed hours — used as an auditing tool to confirm patients provided signatures when required; a patient signature by itself is not a valid EVV compliance measure

Synset.dc:source: Maryland Department of Health, Assistance in Community Integration Services (ACIS) Program Manual (Conflict-Free Case Management), health.maryland.gov/mmcp
Synset.Definition: In Maryland's Assistance in Community Integration Services (ACIS) program, the person-centered care plan developed for each participant upon enrollment; ACIS case managers use it to guide delivery of Tenancy-Based Case Management/Tenancy Support Services and Housing Case Management Services, and the program's conflict-free case management model requires a completed plan for each participant

Synset.dc:source: Michigan DHHS, Home Help — Individual Providers (Final Steps), michigan.gov/mdhhs
Synset.Definition: In Michigan Medicaid's Home Help program, a service-verification method that an individual caregiver submits monthly in the CHAMPS portal (or the MyCare Visit App) to report the specific tasks performed each day for each authorized beneficiary; a separate submission is required for each client served, and caregivers are paid based on the tasks submitted. It is a distinct CHAMPS service-reporting mechanism that coexists with electronic visit verification

Synset.dc:source: National Alliance for Direct Support Professionals, E-Badge Academy (services page) and E-Badge Academy Frequently Asked Questions, nadsp.org
Synset.Definition: A tiered national certification for Direct Support Professionals awarded by the National Alliance for Direct Support Professionals (NADSP) through the E-Badge Academy, a competency-based digital-credentialing platform in which DSPs earn stackable electronic badges by submitting training transcripts and work testimonials; the DSP-I level requires 15 total e-badges, DSP-II a cumulative 30, and DSP-III a cumulative 50, and each certification requires recertification every two years

Under the HCBS Settings Rule, the requirement that a home and community-based setting be integrated in and support full access of individuals receiving Medicaid HCBS to the greater community — including opportunities to seek and work in competitive integrated employment, engage in community life, control personal resources, and receive services in the community — to the same degree of access as individuals not receiving Medicaid HCBS

Synset.dc:source: CMS, Guidance on Settings that have the Effect of Isolating Individuals Receiving HCBS from the Broader Community (2019)
Synset.Definition: A setting whose characteristics have the effect of separating individuals receiving Medicaid HCBS from the broader community — for example, one designed to provide people with disabilities multiple types of services and activities on-site with little interaction with the wider community; CMS identifies such settings by their community-access characteristics rather than by geography, so a rural location does not by itself make a setting isolating

A setting that is not exclusively for people with disabilities; the HCBS Settings Rule requires that an individual be able to select their setting from among options that include such non-disability-specific settings, along with the option of a private unit in a residential setting

A setting the HCBS Settings Rule presumes to have the qualities of an institution, and therefore presumes not to be home and community-based: a setting in a building that also provides inpatient institutional treatment, one on the grounds of or adjacent to a public institution, or any other setting that has the effect of isolating individuals receiving Medicaid HCBS from the broader community; the presumption can be rebutted only through CMS's heightened-scrutiny process

A residential setting that the HCBS provider owns, co-owns, leases, or otherwise controls (which can include a host-home arrangement where the provider controls the residence); in addition to the general HCBS setting qualities, such a setting must meet further conditions under the rule, including a legally enforceable lease or equivalent tenancy protections and rights to privacy, choice, and access

Synset.dc:source: Utah Medicaid (Utah DHHS), HCBS Settings Rule: Community Inclusion & Integration
Synset.Definition: The practice of bringing people and activities from the broader community into a disability-specific setting, rather than supporting the people who live or receive services there to access the broader community; under the HCBS Settings Rule it does not by itself satisfy community integration — visits by community members have value but cannot replace individuals' own access to the community

Synset.dc:source: Consumer Direct Care Network Virginia, FAQ (16-hour work limit; multiple-client application), consumerdirectva.com
Synset.Definition: A daily cap on the hours a personal-care attendant may work; for example, Virginia's consumer-directed Medicaid program limits an attendant to 16 hours of work per day (effective September 1, 2024). The cap is measured per attendant across all of the attendant's clients combined, not per client, so an attendant serving multiple clients cannot work 16 hours for each

Synset.dc:source: Washington DSHS/ALTSA, Overtime Fact Sheet for Individual Providers; Consumer Direct Care Network Washington (Terms and Definitions)
Synset.Definition: In a consumer-directed program, the total number of service hours an Individual Provider may work in a work week (Sunday through Saturday); in Washington State it was established by 2016 state law to control overtime, every Individual Provider has one, and the standard limit is 40 hours

Synset.dc:source: Consumer Direct Care Network Washington, FAQ (Work Week Limit and Client Authorization), consumerdirectwa.com
Synset.Definition: In a consumer-directed program, the portion of a client's authorized service hours assigned (allocated) to a particular Individual Provider to work, used to manage each provider's monthly hours so the total stays within the client's authorized amount; an allocation may not exceed the provider's Work Week Limit

An individual who personally furnishes aide or nursing services under the Medicaid program and is not employed by, contracted with, or affiliated with an agency that provides those services — enrolling directly with Medicaid rather than working through an agency

Synset.dc:source: Oregon Administrative Rules 411-031-0020 (Homecare Worker; Activities of Daily Living)
Synset.Definition: A provider directly employed by a Medicaid consumer to furnish in-home services to that consumer under a consumer-employed provider model (for example, Oregon's Home Care Commission homecare worker); homecare workers assist consumers with activities of daily living — such as eating, dressing, grooming, bathing, personal hygiene, mobility, and toileting — as well as the instrumental activities of daily living needed to continue living independently

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 440.167 (personal care services); 42 CFR 440.70 (home health services)
Synset.Definition: Non-medical, hands-on help with everyday activities — such as bathing, dressing, meals, and homemaking — provided in a person's home (Medicaid personal care services); it differs from home health, which is skilled care (nursing, therapy, or home-health-aide services) furnished only on a physician's or authorized practitioner's orders under a written plan of care

An identifier used to enroll a health care provider and attribute claims to that provider; the federal standard is the National Provider Identifier (NPI), a unique 10-position numeric identifier with no embedded information about the provider, to which Medicaid enrollment records are linked so claims and encounters can be traced to an enrolled, eligible provider

Synset.dc:source: HHS Office of Inspector General, Background Information & Exclusion Authorities, oig.hhs.gov/exclusions
Synset.Definition: The List of Excluded Individuals/Entities — the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General's public database of individuals and entities excluded from participation in federally funded health care programs under section 1128 of the Social Security Act; federal health care programs generally will not pay for items or services furnished, ordered, or prescribed by an excluded party

Synset.dc:source: Texas Health and Human Services Commission, External Medical Review (Texas Medicaid managed-care member materials)
Synset.Definition: In Medicaid managed care, an optional, no-cost step in a member's appeal process in which an Independent Review Organization re-examines an adverse benefit determination (a denied, reduced, or terminated service) based on medical or functional necessity, taken before or alongside a State Fair Hearing — for example, Texas HHSC's External Medical Review

Synset.dc:source: MACPAC, Report to Congress on Medicaid and CHIP (June 2016), ch. 4, Functional Assessments for Long-Term Services and Supports
Synset.Definition: A structured set of questions about an applicant's health conditions and functional needs — such as the ability to perform activities of daily living and the degree of cognitive impairment — that state Medicaid programs use to determine functional eligibility for long-term services and supports and to build a care plan. Distinct from the Functional Assessment Staging Tool (FAST), a dementia-staging scale

Synset.dc:source: 12VAC30-120-924 (Virginia Administrative Code, DMAS home and community-based waiver; skilled respite)
Synset.Definition: Short-term relief care for an unpaid caregiver that includes skilled nursing services, delivered by licensed nursing staff (RN or LPN) under the direct supervision of a licensed, certified, or accredited home health agency and provided on a physician-certified plan of care

Synset.dc:source: 12VAC30-120-924 (Virginia Administrative Code, DMAS home and community-based waiver; unskilled respite)
Synset.Definition: Short-term, non-medical relief care for an unpaid caregiver that provides supervision and assistance with activities of daily living by a personal care aide, and does not include skilled nursing services except for delegable nursing tasks (for example, catheterization)

Family and Medical Leave Act leave that need not be taken in a single continuous block: intermittent leave is FMLA leave taken in separate blocks of time due to a single qualifying reason, while a reduced leave schedule reduces the employee's usual number of working hours per workweek or per workday; both are available when there is a medical need for that arrangement

Synset.dc:source: 42 CFR 438.2 (managed care organization); 42 USC 1396b(l) (EVV applies under fee-for-service and managed care alike)
Synset.Definition: In Medicaid, an entity that has, or is seeking to qualify for, a comprehensive risk contract with the State to deliver a defined benefit package to enrollees; a State that delivers Medicaid benefits through such organizations must comply with the federal managed care regulations at 42 CFR part 438. Electronic visit verification applies to covered personal care and home health services whether they are furnished through a fee-for-service or a managed care delivery system

Synset.dc:source: Netsmart, Mobile Caregiver+ Provider Portal Claims Quick Reference Guide (Work List statuses; voids and adjustments)
Synset.Definition: In electronic visit verification claims processing, the process for correcting visits that do not match a payer's claim rules (unmatched visits) — including when personal-care-service visit data changes; the provider remediates the reported errors on the service record, rematches it so its status becomes Matched, and resubmits the corrected (adjusted) record, since only matched records can be released for payment

Synset.dc:source: Ohio Department of Medicaid, OMES System User Training Guide (GPS Distance Exception Report)
Synset.Definition: In electronic visit verification, an exception raised when a visit's clock-in or clock-out GPS coordinates are captured more than the allowed distance tolerance from the recipient's known service address; such visits are surfaced for review because the recorded location does not match the expected service location

Synset.dc:source: Louisiana Department of Health, Office of Aging and Adult Services, Critical Incidents Reporting Manual (Major Behavioral Incident)
Synset.Definition: A telephone service, such as the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, that provides immediate support during a behavioral-health crisis; in HCBS incident reporting the reportable trigger is the underlying behavioral-health emergency (for example a suicide attempt or suicidal threat), which states classify as a major behavioral incident, rather than the act of placing the call itself

Synset.dc:source: Human Services Research Institute, Root Cause Analysis (prepared for CMS), Some Concepts and Terms
Synset.Definition: In incident management, the most basic and fundamental, or underlying, cause of an adverse event — the root of the problem that must be addressed for prevention strategies to be effective, and in most instances a systems failure rather than human error; it is distinguished from the proximate cause and from contributory factors, and is identified through root cause analysis so the underlying systems failure can be recorded and corrected on the incident report

Synset.dc:source: Iowa Administrative Code, HCBS waiver service providers, definition of "Major incident" (former r. 441—77.37, codification hosted at law.cornell.edu; Iowa recodified its administrative rules effective July 1, 2026)
Synset.Definition: In a state HCBS waiver's incident-reporting rules, a defined category of reportable occurrence during service provision — for example, in Iowa, an occurrence that results in a physical injury to or by the member requiring a physician's treatment or admission to a hospital, the member's death, a need for emergency mental health treatment, or the intervention of law enforcement; a member seen by a primary care physician for an injury requiring the physician's treatment can meet the major-incident threshold even without an emergency room visit

Synset.dc:source: Louisiana Department of Health, Office of Aging and Adult Services, Critical Incidents Reporting Manual (Major injury)
Synset.Definition: An injury whose cause is not known; state HCBS incident rules generally make it reportable only when it requires treatment by a physician, dentist, nurse, or other licensed health care provider, so minor injuries such as small bruises or scrapes that do not require such treatment do not meet the reporting threshold

As a reportable HCBS incident category, an incident that results in an individual being tased, arrested, charged, or incarcerated; law enforcement merely being called to and speaking with a member, without any of those outcomes, does not by itself rise to the level of reportable law enforcement intervention

Synset.dc:source: Iowa Administrative Code, HCBS waiver service providers, definition of "Major incident" (former r. 441—77.37, criterion requiring emergency mental health treatment; codification hosted at law.cornell.edu; Iowa recodified its rules effective July 1, 2026)
Synset.Definition: In a state HCBS waiver's incident-reporting rules, urgent, unscheduled mental health treatment for a member occurring during service provision — a defined trigger for a reportable major incident; the rule establishes the category but does not itemize the specific interventions that constitute the treatment

Synset.dc:source: Wisconsin Department of Health Services, Electronic Visit Verification (EVV): Providers and Independent Nurses
Synset.Definition: A nurse enrolled as an individual Medicaid provider — rather than through an agency — who delivers Medicaid-funded in-home nursing services; independent nurses are subject to electronic visit verification and must verify their service visits through an EVV system, following the same setup steps as agency providers

Synset.dc:source: Illinois Department of Human Services, Division of Developmental Disabilities, Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Policy
Synset.Definition: The home- and community-based personal care and home health services delivered under a developmental-disabilities 1915(c) waiver that are subject to electronic visit verification — in Illinois, services by Personal Support Workers, occupational, physical, and speech therapists, and licensed practical or registered nurses; residential-habilitation settings such as Community Integrated Living Arrangements and Community Day Services are excluded from the EVV requirement

Synset.dc:source: 16 DE Admin. Code 3220 (Training and Qualifications for Certified Nursing Assistants), Reciprocity
Synset.Definition: The process by which a nurse aide trained and certified in another state obtains certification to work in a given state; a person cannot work as a certified nursing assistant on an out-of-state certificate alone but may qualify through reciprocity by holding a current certificate in good standing in their home jurisdiction and meeting recent work-experience or equivalent training-and-competency requirements

The status of a nurse-aide certification that has not been renewed within the allowed period; in Delaware a nurse-aide certification must be renewed every two years and may be renewed up to 30 days past expiration with a penalty fee, after which it is deemed lapsed and the individual is not permitted to work as a certified nursing assistant until they reapply and pass the CNA competency test

Synset.dc:source: Public Partnerships (PPL), New York CDPAP Frequently Asked Questions
Synset.Definition: In some consumer-directed programs, a rule paying a personal assistant the 1.5x overtime rate for work performed on the seventh day when the assistant works all seven days of the pay-period week (Sunday to Saturday) for a non-relative consumer, even if the assistant did not reach 40 hours that week

Synset.dc:source: Public Partnerships (PPL), New York CDPAP Frequently Asked Questions
Synset.Definition: The rule that a personal assistant or attendant may not claim or be paid for service hours while the consumer is a hospital inpatient or in another institutional or healthcare facility, except for the date of admission and the date of discharge

Synset.dc:source: Public Partnerships (PPL), New York CDPAP FAQ; Consumer Direct Care Network Virginia, What Is Consumer-Direction?
Synset.Definition: A self-directed model of Medicaid home care in which the consumer (or their representative) recruits, hires, trains, and supervises their own personal assistants and is not required to join a home-care agency, in contrast to an agency-directed model in which an agency employs and assigns the caregiver

Synset.dc:source: Consumer Direct Care Network Washington, FAQ (Work Week Limit and Client Authorization)
Synset.Definition: In a consumer-directed Medicaid program, the total service hours a client may receive in a month; the hours are authorized to the financial-management or employer-of-record entity rather than to individual providers, and are viewable by the client's managing employer (the client or their authorized representative) in the program's web portal

Synset.dc:source: Public Partnerships (PPL), New York CDPAP Frequently Asked Questions
Synset.Definition: In New York's Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program (CDPAP), the rule that a personal assistant does not need a certificate or license to serve; the consumer-directed model allows consumers to hire and train their own personal assistants without professional certification

Synset.dc:source: Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services (DMAS), Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) Frequently Asked Questions
Synset.Definition: In electronic visit verification, two caregivers' shifts for the same client may not have overlapping paid time; because reporting is at the minute level, one aide clocking out and another clocking in within the same minute is acceptable, but genuinely overlapping paid time is not

Synset.dc:source: Consumer Direct Care Network Washington (mileage submission; Terms and Definitions)
Synset.Definition: In Washington's CDWA program, the submission of an individual provider's mileage for reimbursement; mileage is submitted through the DirectMyCare web portal or the IVR phone system, not through the CareAttend app, which is used only for clocking in and out

Synset.dc:source: 42 USC 1396b(l)(1); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions: Section 12006 of the 21st Century Cures Act EVV Systems for PCS and HHCS (May 2018)
Synset.Definition: Electronic visit verification is a data-verification requirement, not a service-authorization or location-gatekeeping mechanism: it electronically verifies that an already-authorized personal care or home health visit occurred (who, what, when, and where), and does not itself restrict where a beneficiary may go or what they may do in the community

Whether an employee has worked the 1,250 hours of service needed for FMLA eligibility is determined according to the Fair Labor Standards Act's principles for compensable hours of work — the actual number of hours the employee has worked for the employer, not limited by recordkeeping methods or compensation agreements that do not accurately reflect hours actually worked; because only hours actually worked count as hours of service, paid time the employee did not actually work — vacation, sick leave, or other paid time off — does not count toward the 1,250-hour threshold

To support FMLA leave for a serious health condition, an employer may require the employee to submit a certification issued by a health care provider — a professional statement covering matters such as the date the condition began, its probable duration, and relevant medical facts — not the employee's underlying medical records themselves; an employer is not entitled to demand the records directly

Synset.dc:source: 29 USC 2611(14) (a well-established FMLA statutory definition, consistent with the already-cited hc-fmla-qualifying-exigency-leave and hc-fmla-military-leave-types glosses in this file)
Synset.Definition: For FMLA qualifying-exigency leave, "covered active duty" means, for a member of a regular component of the Armed Forces, duty during the deployment of the member with the Armed Forces to a foreign country; for a member of a reserve component, it means duty during such deployment under a call or order to active duty in support of a contingency operation

Synset.dc:source: 29 USC 2611(15) (a well-established FMLA statutory definition, consistent with the already-cited hc-fmla-military-caregiver-leave gloss in this file)
Synset.Definition: For FMLA military caregiver leave, a "covered servicemember" is a current member of the Armed Forces — including a member of the National Guard or Reserves, and so including a member of the Regular Armed Forces — who is undergoing medical treatment, recuperation, or therapy, is in outpatient status, or is on the temporary disability retired list, for a serious injury or illness, or a covered veteran undergoing medical treatment, recuperation, or therapy for a serious injury or illness

Synset.dc:source: 29 CFR 825.122(c)-(d) (a well-established FMLA regulatory definition, consistent with the already-cited hc-fmla-covered-family-member gloss in this file)
Synset.Definition: For FMLA leave to care for a family member, "son or daughter" is defined to include a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, or a child of a person standing in loco parentis; correspondingly, "parent" is defined to include a biological, adoptive, step, or foster parent, or an individual who stood in loco parentis to the employee — so a stepson or stepdaughter of a covered servicemember, and a stepparent of a covered servicemember, each fall within these definitions for purposes of FMLA leave

Under Medicaid self-direction, an authorized participant's services are funded from the participant's Medicaid-approved individual budget, administered through a financial management services entity that processes payroll and pays invoices for approved goods and services from that budget; the participant/employer does not pay for the Medicaid-authorized services out of their own pocket

Synset.dc:source: Iowa HHS, Frequently Asked Questions: Recognizing and Reporting Incidents for HCBS Members (last updated 11/8/2024), hhs.iowa.gov/media/15047/download (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: When a member falls at home and EMS is called for assistance but the member is not transported to a hospital, a major (critical) incident report is generally not required, because the occurrence did not result in a physical injury requiring treatment from a medical professional or admission to a hospital; a minor incident report may still be required if EMS provided basic first aid

Synset.dc:source: Iowa HHS, Frequently Asked Questions: Recognizing and Reporting Incidents for HCBS Members (last updated 11/8/2024), hhs.iowa.gov/media/15047/download (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: When a member falls, goes to the emergency room, and has x-rays taken, a critical incident report is required regardless of whether a fracture is found: the presence or absence of a fracture does not decide reportability, and treatment at an emergency room is itself "treatment from a medical professional," which is what triggers the requirement

Synset.dc:source: Iowa HHS, Frequently Asked Questions: Recognizing and Reporting Incidents for HCBS Members (last updated 11/8/2024), hhs.iowa.gov/media/15047/download (fetched 2026-07-24)
Synset.Definition: A walk-in clinic, rapid-care, or urgent-care visit for medical treatment of a physical injury counts as "treatment from a medical professional" for critical-incident reporting purposes, so a critical incident report is required on the same basis as an emergency-room visit

Where a self-direction program participant is a minor, a Central Registry background-check finding of child abuse or neglect against a prospective attendant bars that attendant from receiving Medicaid payment to work for the family
